THE Government will seek to have itself removed from any list of countries flagged by the United States for excess production capacity, as Washington weighs a proposed 100 per cent tariff on imported semiconductors.
Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani said Malaysia had received no indication that the US intended to impose tariffs on its semiconductor exports, but discussions under Section 301 remained unresolved over excess capacity.
“So far, there is no indication that the US will impose any tariffs on semiconductors from Malaysia,” he told a press conference at EU-Malaysia Business Day 2026 held in Kuala Lumpur on Tuesday.
Johari said excess production capacity was the only outstanding issue among four areas raised in the trade discussions, which also covered forced labour, environmental standards and government subsidies.
He said Malaysia would ask Washington to identify the countries it considered to have excess capacity, arguing that any such problem associated with Malaysia could originate from third countries.
“Malaysia will request a list of countries identified as having excess capacity so that we can seek to have those countries removed from the list,” he said.
Johari said Malaysia had no issues concerning environmental standards or government subsidies, adding that the country did not subsidise companies to export products to international markets and complied with environmental standards set by developed economies.
US President Donald Trump had proposed imposing a 100 per cent tariff on imported semiconductor chips, raising concerns over potential trade barriers for chip-exporting economies such as Malaysia.
Johari said exporters had to meet the laws and requirements of their destination markets.
“Any market we want to enter has its own criteria and laws that must be complied with. If we do not comply, we cannot enter that market,” he added. - October 13, 2026

articles.title: How China Plus One Is Transforming ASEAN Trade - Global Finance Magazine
articles.summary: How China Plus One Is Transforming ASEAN Trade  Global Finance Magazine
articles.full_text:
Supply-chain diversification fuels a growing Southeast Asian financial ecosystem.
This article appears in the October issue of Global Finance Magazine.
China Plus One (C+1) is a supply-chain-focused strategy in which companies retain substantial manufacturing and sourcing in China while adding at least one other country. The C+1 strategy is rapidly shifting manufacturing to countries in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), boosting foreign direct investment (FDI), expanding trade surpluses, and driving GDP growth.
At the same time, the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP)—a free trade agreement among 10 ASEAN member countries plus Australia, China, Japan, New Zealand, and the Republic of Korea—is boosting intraregional trade and the cross-border use of local currencies, thereby germinating a potentially formidable Southeast Asian financial ecosystem.
China’s unmatched supplier density, scale, and infrastructure are retained, but concentration risk is mitigated by building capacity in ASEAN (or elsewhere). If a manufacturing site or supplier faces a tariff hike, lockdown, or political shock, production can shift rather than halt. Even without these factors, costs are substantially reduced.
A clear example of C+1 in action is Taiwan’s Foxconn, which operates factories in Bac Ninh Province in northern Vietnam, where its plant assembles Apple’s AirPods and MacBooks using high-value parts manufactured in China.
The industrial base remains in China, with ASEAN serving as a tariff and resilience hedge. Vietnam has benefited from a cumulative $5 billion in Foxconn’s FDI in the country from 2007-2026—according to Taiwan Stock Exchange and Bac Ninh local government data—to create manufacturing capacity and more than 100,000 jobs in Vietnam.
The FDI story exemplified by Foxconn has been echoed across ASEAN. “Since 2021, FDI in the region has been exceptionally strong, with annual inflows exceeding $200 billion, compared with an annual average during the last decade of less than $130 billion,” according to the ASEAN Investment Report 2025, published last October by the ASEAN Secretariat and the UN Conference for Trade and Development (UNCTAD).
That report tallies 2024 inflows at $226 billion. Underlining the ASEAN dynamic in relative global terms, FDI was up by 8.5% that year while global FDI fell 11%.
“The strategic importance of ASEAN in global supply chains has strengthened significantly over the past decade, catalyzed by the China Plus One strategy, which aims to mitigate risks arising from geopolitical tensions and search for more-resilient production networks,” said Han Teng Chua and Radhika Rao, senior economists at DBS.
“The region’s open and foreign-investor-friendly policies, coupled with companies’ efforts to expand markets, diversify risks, and optimize costs, could drive ASEAN-6’s FDI inflows to grow at a robust CAGR of 7% over the next decade.” ASEAN-6 is a bloc comprising Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam.
Funding the Trade Finance Gap
Alongside the FDI narrative sit two burning issues: the pressing need to finance ASEAN trade, which is characterized by an “unmet gap” between demand and trade finance; and the underpinning of the region’s economies by micro, small, and midsize enterprises (MSMEs) and SMEs.
A joint assessment by the U.K. Growth Gateway and Boston Consulting Group, dated February 2024, puts the ASEAN-specific unmet gap at roughly $350 billion to $400 billion and estimates that closing even 10%-20% of that gap could unlock $85 billion to $105 billion in “trade value uplift” and about 6 million jobs in the region’s trade-related industries.
But a big reason for the region’s unmet gap is the preponderance of SMEs and MSMEs. According to the ASEAN Secretariat, these account for 97.2% to 99.9% of all business establishments. Collectively, SMEs and MSMEs generate about 85% of employment, contribute 44.8% of GDP, and supply 18% of national exports, making them central to job creation, inclusive growth, and value-added activity across both urban and rural areas.
The sobering fact is that about 40% of these companies’ trade-finance applications are rejected, according to the Asian Development Bank (ADB), often because applicants lack sufficient collateral, complete documentation, or an established credit history.
This is compounded by ASEAN’s fragmented nature and the urgent need to fully digitize trade and trade finance in a region that still relies on paper documentation. The Model Law on Electronic Transferable Records (MLETR) is the solution: a legal template that ASEAN countries can incorporate into law so that a digital original of trade documents has the same legal status as a paper original.
Singapore implemented MLETR in 2021, and the hope is that ASEAN’s Digital Economy Framework Agreement will push the rest of the region to align with it.
“Carbon copies still choke ASEAN trade—slow ships, costly credit, shut-out SMEs. MLETR is the legal unlock. Singapore is live. Mass uptake isn’t guaranteed, but the shift would be seismic,” said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for Asia Pacific at Natixis, in Hong Kong.
Singapore’s move came in preparation for the RCEP, which came into force in 2022 for the first 10 ratifying countries. The 15 RCEP member countries represent the world’s largest trade bloc by population and economic size—about 30% of global population and GDP.
The RCEP aims to cut tariffs on more than 90% of goods traded among its members by 2042 and also covers services, investment, e-commerce, and intellectual property. Intra-RCEP trade rose sharply in 2022 to around $1 trillion and stood at around $6 trillion last year. The agreement has positively impacted trade for Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, and Vietnam with other RCEP partners—exports from Cambodia to RCEP countries account for more than 60% of the country’s total trade.
Rebuilding ASEAN’s Trade Plumbing
Digitalized supply-chain finance—anchored in distributed-ledger technology—and local-currency settlement can rebuild ASEAN’s trade plumbing around firms, not just banks. Anchor buyers channel liquidity to SME and MSME suppliers, bypassing the need for collateral and thereby helping to fill the unmet gap.
The ADB’s Trade and Supply Chain Finance Program (TSCFP) helps close the unmet gap in SME trade finance by issuing AAA-rated guarantees and loans through more than 250 partner banks, enabling smaller firms in developing Asia to import, export, and access supply-chain working capital that private lenders would otherwise typically withhold.
In August, Steven Beck, TSCFP director, relocated to Singapore, in a move that reflects the city-state’s preeminence as an ASEAN supply-chain and trade-finance hub. “Being here means we can work much more closely in this energized ecosystem, feeding off the energy and exchanging ideas in a way you just can’t do remotely,” he said.
“It’s been a remarkable year,” Beck added. “Our business is up over 60% compared to the same period last year, which is a huge jump for a program that already supports about 20,000 transactions worth over $5 billion annually. Part of that is just persistent, unmet demand for trade finance in markets that have historically been underserved.”
Settling invoices through ASEAN’s Local Currency Transaction Framework alleviates dollar scarcity that bedevils the trade arena in smaller ASEAN economies and reduces foreign exchange spreads and correspondent-bank delays that hinder SME and MSME exporters. Linked digital platforms—e-invoicing, QR-code payment networks, and regional payment connectivity—convert those flows into reusable credit data. The result is a tighter, cheaper intra-ASEAN financial ecosystem in which trade transactions themselves become the collateral.
Jonathan Rogers is a contributing writer based in Vietnam.

articles.title: Behind the windfall profits of Vietnam’s rubber companies - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Behind the windfall profits of Vietnam’s rubber companies  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Rubber prices have climbed to a 13-year high, boosting prospects for latex producers. But sharp profit increases at some companies have also been driven by plantation clearance and, in particular, income from land conversions.
Global rubber prices have remained elevated after hitting a 13-year high. According to the Vietnam Commodity Exchange (MXV), the November contract for TSR20 rubber reached $2,548 per ton on September 30, its highest level since May 2013.
Trading Economics data show that rubber prices continued to rise in October. As of October 14, the price tracked by the platform had increased more than 50% from a year earlier to 265.4 U.S. cents per kg, equivalent to $2,654 per ton.
The market had expected supply to become more abundant in the third quarter, as rubber trees completed their annual leaf-shedding cycle and resumed latex tapping, potentially easing prices. However, supply concerns have persisted, with heavy rain in some Southeast Asian producing regions disrupting harvesting.
This trend is also reflected in the actual selling prices achieved by Vietnamese companies. Dong Phu Rubber JSC (HoSE: DPR) reported an average selling price of VND62.13 million ($2,400) per ton in September, lifting its average price for the year to VND57.83 million per ton, up more than 14% from the same period last year.
Brokerages have also forecast strong profit growth across the rubber sector. SSI Securities expects after-tax profit at Phuoc Hoa Rubber JSC (HoSE: PHR) to rise 233.6% in 2026 from 2025, while DPR's profit is projected to increase 121% and that of Vietnam Rubber Group (HoSE: GVR) 33.9%.
For Tay Ninh Rubber JSC (HoSE: TRC), brokerage MBS forecasts net profit of VND659 billion ($25.46 million) in 2026, up 163% from the previous year. In a report dated October 8, the brokerage said selling prices, latex sales volumes and land compensation would all support business results.
A common thread in these forecasts is that higher latex prices are improving operating performance, while income from plantation clearance and land-related payments could accelerate profit growth. The contribution and timing of each revenue source will therefore determine how quickly individual companies' earnings grow.
Latex remains the mainstay
Higher selling prices are helping rubber companies boost revenue and profitability. DPR sold 11,351 tons of rubber in the first nine months of the year, up 29.4% from a year earlier. Combined with a September selling price above VND62 million ($2,400) per ton, the increase in sales volumes indicates that the company is benefiting from both higher prices and stronger demand.
Reviewed semi-annual consolidated financial statements highlight latex's role in gross profit. At GVR, rubber production and trading generated around VND3.64 trillion (VND140.62 million) in gross profit in the first half of 2026, accounting for 80.8% of the group's consolidated gross profit. It remained the largest contributor among the group's business activities.
At DPR, rubber production and trading generated VND143.1 billion ($5.53 million) in gross profit, up 65.7% year on year. Its share of total gross profit increased to 55.4% from 53.2%. At PHR, rubber products generated VND225.7 billion in gross profit, up 43.2%, accounting for 88.2% of the total. The segment's gross margin also improved to around 27.2% from 25.5%.
MBS also has a positive outlook for TRC. The brokerage forecasts its average selling price in 2026 to rise 17% from 2025, while rubber revenue is expected to increase 33%. Plantations in Vietnam and Cambodia are expected to support output, with the Cambodian acreage entering a period of higher yields.
Nevertheless, elevated prices have not eliminated market uncertainties. Trading Economics has flagged weak demand in China. Natural rubber prices are also affected by petroleum-based synthetic rubber, particularly when oil prices fall. For domestic producers, the benefits will depend on tapping volumes, product mix and costs. Overall, however, rubber companies are benefiting from the current market environment.
Other sources of income
Plantation clearance and land conversion are generating significant additional profits for rubber companies. However, accounting treatment differs: some proceeds are included in gross profit, while others are recorded as other income.
At DPR, revenue from the sale of cleared rubber trees reached VND107.4 billion ($4.15 million) in the first half, against costs of around VND7.3 billion. The resulting margin of VND100.1 billion ($3.87 million) was included in gross profit from rubber tree liquidation and wood processing. This source accounted for 38.7% of consolidated gross profit, alongside 55.4% from latex.
DPR's September report showed that the cumulative area of rubber plantations cleared for liquidation reached 576 hectares, exceeding the full-year target by 39.1% and increasing 25.5% from a year earlier. This progress is opening up an additional source of income from plantations, although the actual profit contribution depends on recognition timing and related costs.
According to VCBS, DPR could also benefit from around VND473 billion ($18.27 million) in compensation related to 1,411.6 hectares of land for a high-tech agricultural project in Dong Nai province. The brokerage estimates that proceeds from rubber tree liquidation could reach VND300 billion to VND400 billion. These remain expectations contingent on project progress and represent non-recurring income.
At PHR, land-related proceeds are clearly reflected in other income. In the first half, the company recorded VND323.4 billion ($12.49 million) related to VSIP III and VND171.7 billion in compensation and support payments for land acquired for a specialized mechanical engineering industrial park.
After deducting other expenses, PHR's other profit reached VND496.3 billion, equivalent to 61.6% of its pre-tax profit, compared with only around 2% in the first half of 2025. Together with improved gross profit from rubber, this income helped consolidated after-tax profit rise nearly 232% to VND655.3 billion ($24.31 million).
Land-related income does not always have the same characteristics. The compensation and support payment associated with VSIP III, in particular, is calculated based on 20% of gross profit generated from areas that the partner leases to end customers under sublease contracts. The amount recognised therefore depends on leasing results in each period.
At the group level, GVR reported other profit of over VND2,095 billion ($80.91 million) in the first half, accounting for nearly 36% of consolidated pre-tax profit. Other income mainly comprised VND1,028 billion ($39.71 million) from rubber trees cleared for liquidation or damaged by falling, and 955.7 billion in compensation and support payments for losses. Thus, while latex remains the mainstay of gross profit, non-latex income continues to make a substantial contribution to overall results.
However, proceeds from land and tree compensation are typically one-off items recognised at particular points in time.
TRC provides a clear example of the impact of recognition timing. MBS expects the company to receive around VND400 billion in land compensation related to Hiep Thanh Industrial Park in the fourth quarter of 2026. Under this assumption, net profit would rise 163% in 2026 but fall around 33% in 2027 to VND440 billion ($17 million), as a comparable compensation payment would no longer be available.
Despite the overall decline in profit, MBS still forecasts TRC's gross profit from rubber operations to increase around 7% in 2027. Excluding compensation and proceeds from clearing plantations for land conversion, the brokerage projects net profit growth of 37% in 2026 and 8% in 2027. Changes in a company's overall earnings may therefore differ from the performance of its latex business.
Similarly, SSI forecasts DPR's after-tax profit to fall 17.1% in 2027, while PHR and GVR are expected to post further increases of around 12% and 10%, respectively. These differences show that favorable rubber prices do not necessarily translate into the same pace of profit growth across the sector.
To assess whether an exceptional year can be sustained, investors need to monitor selling prices, volumes and latex margins alongside land handover schedules, plantation clearance and the recognition of compensation payments. A year of sharply higher profits driven by land and tree compensation can produce impressive financial statements, but such income is not guaranteed to recur.
At the same time, a reduction in plantation acreage could weigh on long-term tapping volumes if companies do not have corresponding plans to replant or expand their cultivated areas.

In particular, investments from FDI capital flows reflect the long-term vision and confidence of Japanese businesses in the potential for sustainable economic growth in Vietnam and the region.
Highlights of investment cooperation
In fact, a bright spot in Vietnam-Japan economic relations has been investment cooperation, a prime example over the past several years. According to statistics from the Trade Promotion Agency of the Ministry of Industry and Trade , Japan has over 5,800 active projects in Vietnam with a total investment capital exceeding US$81 billion. Simultaneously, numerous Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) continue to facilitate businesses in both countries in terms of tariffs, rules of origin, and trade facilitation, expanding opportunities for deeper participation in regional supply chains and production networks.

For example, OJI Group, Japan, recently commenced construction of a new aseptic carton packaging plant in Vietnam under the Oji Liquid Pak (OLP) brand, with a total investment of US$110 million, at the Long Thanh High-Tech Park, Dong Nai province. The project demonstrates Oji Liquid Pak's long-term investment commitment in Vietnam, while also affirming Vietnam's strategic role as a manufacturing and supply hub in the Group's growth strategy in Southeast Asia, contributing to the region's shift towards circular packaging solutions and meeting policy requirements.
Mr. Nguyen Quoc An, Deputy Head of the Management Board of Industrial Parks and Economic Zones of Dong Nai City (DNIEZA), stated that large-scale projects like these not only contribute to promoting the development of the local industry but also create opportunities to enhance domestic production capacity and strengthen Vietnam's participation in the regional supply chain. The Management Board of Industrial Parks and Economic Zones of Dong Nai City commits to continuing to support and facilitate investors throughout the project implementation process, within its assigned functions, duties, and authority; promptly guiding and coordinating the resolution of any difficulties and obstacles that arise so that the project is implemented in accordance with regulations and can commence operations as soon as possible.
Mr. Kestutis Sliuzas, General Director of Oji Liquid Pak, shared that more and more manufacturing industries, including the packaging industry, are shifting to a new standard where efficiency, food safety, operational flexibility, and circular economy elements must go hand in hand. Therefore, the Oji Liquid Pak Co., Ltd. factory project combines the production of packaging for the food industry with research and development, technical services, installation, and maintenance of Japanese-made machinery, thereby contributing to the goal of creating a modern, high-quality, and high-value-added production environment in the industrial park.

According to some experts, besides manufacturing, Japanese FDI flows into diverse fields such as research and development in natural sciences; repair, maintenance, and installation of machinery and equipment; and import, export, and distribution of goods in accordance with Vietnamese law . Mr. Tran Viet Ha, Deputy Head of the Ho Chi Minh City Export Processing Zones and Industrial Parks Management Board (HEPZA), stated that facilitating investors' early project implementation after registration and reducing procedures related to planning and construction are the goals that HEPZA is focusing on currently and in the near future. On the other hand, Resolution No. 10-NQ/TW dated June 8, 2026, of the Politburo on the development of the foreign-invested economy also sets out an important policy direction, shifting the strategic focus of Vietnam's investment attraction from prioritizing the quantity of foreign investment to emphasizing quality, specifically investments that bring high technology, innovation, human resource development, and technology transfer. Vietnam is no longer a destination for simple assembly activities based on cheap labor, but is positioning itself as a center for high value-added, technology-based investment.
Corporate responsibility
Entering a new era, with a strong shift from attracting investment based on quantity to attracting selective investment, many industrial parks in localities such as Ho Chi Minh City, Dong Nai, etc., are prioritizing projects with advanced technology, high added value, efficient land use, environmental friendliness, and the ability to participate in and enhance the locality's position in domestic and global supply chains. In this orientation, many industrial parks also demonstrate a particularly important role in creating space to accommodate projects with high quality, advanced technology and management methods, especially those demonstrating corporate responsibility towards the environment and the community.

Mr. ONO Masuo further informed that the Vietnamese government has set clear economic growth targets towards 2030, and the process of improving institutions and infrastructure is progressing steadily. In addition, the living conditions and working environment of the people are constantly changing, especially in ensuring the legitimate rights of workers.

Entering the next phase of its development, Kao Vietnam aims to continue delivering new value to consumers, not only through strengthening its brand and products, but also by promoting initiatives that contribute to solving social problems in Vietnam. This is also part of the company's long-term and sustainable development strategy, with a desire to find ways to enhance corporate responsibility and contribute more to the local community.

articles.title: Malaysia’s Budget 2027 semiconductor push leans on state investors as Khazanah and KWAP double chip funding - Tech Wire Asia
articles.summary: Malaysia’s Budget 2027 semiconductor push leans on state investors as Khazanah and KWAP double chip funding  Tech Wire Asia
articles.full_text:
- TNB adds RM15 billion to the grid that chipmakers and data centres rely on
Malaysia’s Budget 2027 semiconductor measures put government-linked investors at the centre, with Khazanah Nasional and the Retirement Fund (Incorporated), or KWAP, committing RM1.2 billion to help local chip companies move into higher-value segments, according to the budget speech Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim delivered on 9 October.
The two funds committed RM550 million to the semiconductor ecosystem in Budget 2026, aimed at strengthening partnerships between local firms and multinationals, according to The Star’s summary of last year’s measures.
Where the Budget 2027 semiconductor money sits
The RM1.2 billion forms part of RM25 billion in domestic investment that government-linked investment companies (GLICs) will mobilise under the GEAR-uP programme, the speech said. It includes a partnership between Khazanah and the Selangor state government on an investment fund to develop the state’s semiconductor industry. The speech did not say how much of the RM1.2 billion goes to that fund.
In its section on Penang, the speech said Khazanah and InvestPenang will set up a RM100 million Strategic Investment Fund to back semiconductor and advanced manufacturing companies in their early stages of growth, with Penang positioned as the country’s technology finance centre. Development bank BPMB will allocate RM7 billion across seven strategic sectors, including semiconductors.
The Malaysian Technology Development Corporation’s SemiconStart programme will provide follow-on equity for start-ups in IC design, advanced packaging and semiconductor materials, though the speech gave no amount. SemiconStart launched in July with a first cohort of 10 companies, with selected companies able to receive incubation support of up to RM1 million each, Business Today reported.
Moving beyond assembly and testing
Malaysia holds about 13% of the global market for semiconductor assembly, testing and packaging, according to The Edge. The National Semiconductor Strategy, launched in 2024, sets out the shift beyond that base. When Anwar announced at least RM25 billion in fiscal support for the strategy in May 2024, the targets included at least RM500 billion in investment in its first phase, at least 10 local design and advanced packaging companies with revenues of RM1 billion to RM4.7 billion, and 60,000 trained engineers, according to MIDA.
Tengku Zafrul Abdul Aziz, chairman of the Malaysian Investment Development Authority, said local firms needed to turn the budget allocation into more work in higher-value areas such as IC design. “The ecosystem is quite mature, but we need to strengthen the way we are in that value chain,” he said on Bernama TV’s The Nation on 14 October, Malay Mailreported. He added that manufacturing projects could take about two years from groundbreaking to completed factories, depending on the industry.
Before the budget, Apex Securities expected targeted measures for the sector rather than one large semiconductor allocation, according to The Edge on 5 October. The brokerage’s checks with Penang companies found AI-driven demand holding strong into 2027 and 2028, with firms running near full capacity and facing long equipment lead times, input shortages and difficulty retaining engineers.
Power and data centres behind the chip push
The speech said Tenaga Nasional Bhd (TNB) would invest RM15 billion to strengthen the national grid to meet electricity demand. Tax incentives for green technology were enhanced and extended to 31 December 2030. A RM1.25 billion New Economy Venture Fund set up by Sime Darby Property, the Employees Provident Fund and the Armed Forces Fund Board (LTAT) will develop data centres and industrial logistics assets in Elmina, Selangor. The government is also planning a sovereign AI cloud to keep national data under Malaysian control, though the speech gave no allocation for it.
Cheam Tat Inn, managing director of Equinix Malaysia, said the grid investment and the green incentive extension reinforce the need to align digital infrastructure growth with long-term energy readiness. “As digital infrastructure expands, energy efficiency, water stewardship and infrastructure readiness must remain central considerations,” he said in commentary on the budget.
Wong Weng Yew, managing director of Open DC and group managing director of Extreme Broadband, said the Penang fund pointed to rising demand for digital infrastructure in the north. The fund “sends a clear signal of growing demand for the digital infrastructure these industries depend on,” he said. Open DC is scaling its PE2 facility in Penang in phases towards 100MW, sized to contracted demand, he added.
The US tariff question
Four days after the budget, Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Johari Abdul Ghani said Malaysian semiconductor exports to the US remain exempt from tariffs. “We have not received any indication that the US will impose tariffs on Malaysian semiconductors at this time,” he said, according to The Edge.
In the wider trade talks with the US, Johari said the only issue not yet finalised was excess capacity, which he attributed to goods originating from third countries.

articles.title: India ready to co-produce defence equipment with ASEAN countries: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh - The New Indian Express
articles.summary: India ready to co-produce defence equipment with ASEAN countries: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh  The New Indian Express
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI: India is ready to co-develop and co-produce defence equipment with ASEAN countries, including patrol vessels, radars, air-defence systems, helicopters and drones, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said on Wednesday.
He presented the country as a long-term industrial partner for Southeast Asia rather than just an arms supplier.
Addressing the first ASEAN-India Defence Think Tank Forum at the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses (MP-IDSA), Singh said such cooperation would be tailored to each country's needs and priorities.
"Self-reliance does not mean working in isolation," he said.
The Aatmanirbhar Bharat initiative, he added, could create opportunities for "trusted partners to design, build, maintain and improve equipment together".
Co-development, co-production, maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO), training and long-term technical support "can build local skills, support industry and make supply chains more reliable", he said.
"Our researchers need to look closely at what makes such partnerships work: clear requirements, reliable after-sales support, appropriate technology safeguards, fair sharing of responsibilities and benefits, and opportunities for local companies and skilled workers. Our goal should be lasting partnerships, not one-time transactions," Singh added.
The offer comes as India's defence footprint in the region grows. The Philippines became the first foreign buyer of the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile, signing a $375 million deal in 2022. Vietnam's BrahMos contract, worth about $630 million, was confirmed in May.
Indonesia signed for the missile in July during Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to Jakarta, along with an agreement for Astra air-to-air missiles. All three countries have disputes with China in the South China Sea.
Without naming any country, Singh said the region was changing rapidly amid growing strategic competition and pressure created at times through actions at sea. He also cited threats such as terrorism, cybercrime, piracy, trafficking and illegal fishing.
"India seeks an Indo-Pacific where all countries, large and small, make their own choices, protect their interests and pursue development in peace," he said.
He called for a regional order in which countries are not forced to choose sides.
Pointing out that the current year has been designated the ASEAN-India Year of Maritime Cooperation, Singh called for stronger maritime domain awareness, interoperability and underwater cooperation.
“We should improve the sharing of maritime information, strengthen cooperation among our navies and coast guards, and build the ability to respond together to emergencies," he said.
On emerging technology, he said recent conflicts had shown that relatively low-cost drones can challenge expensive defence systems.
He proposed joint work on counter-drone systems, cyber defence, maritime surveillance and disaster response. Start-ups, universities and smaller firms could take part through platforms such as Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) and the Technology Development Fund (TDF).

articles.title: China on cusp of US$1 trillion trade surplus as exports surge - The Business Times
articles.summary: China on cusp of US$1 trillion trade surplus as exports surge  The Business Times
articles.full_text:
Shipments abroad soar 36% in September from a year earlier and imports jump 31%
[BEIJING] China’s trade surplus ballooned to US$938 billion for the first nine months, keeping it on pace to exceed 2025’s record as export growth surged faster than expected in September.
The country’s export growth surged the most since February to drive global trade imbalances to new highs, with its surplus in the first nine months of the year on track to exceed the US$1.2 trillion record set in 2025.
Shipments abroad soared 36 per cent last month from a year earlier and imports jumped 31 per cent, data released by China’s General Administration of Customs showed on Wednesday (Oct 14).
As a result, the trade surplus for September widened to almost US$134 billion, exceeding every forecast in a Bloomberg survey of economists.
The year-to-date measure of the difference between what China exports and what it imports is already at US$938 billion – almost 8 per cent more than during the same period last year.
Surging prices for chips and commodities like oil and metals have inflated China’s trade figures, with exports and imports rising less in volume terms.
Prices at the factory gate exceeded most estimates and jumped 5 per cent in September from a year earlier, reaching their fastest since 2022, according to data published by the National Bureau of Statistics on Wednesday.
“China’s September trade data delivered another upside surprise,” said Zhou Hao, chief economist at Guotai Junan. The size of the monthly trade surplus “underscores the continued strength of China’s external sector despite lingering concerns over domestic demand”.
China’s lopsided trade relations with the world have grown even more extreme since the tariff war started by US President Donald Trump over a year ago, especially as global demand exploded for artificial-intelligence services and inputs like chips.
Shipments of high-tech products soared almost 64 per cent in September, which Bloomberg Economics estimates contributed around half of China’s total export growth.
Facing higher barriers in the US, Chinese companies have sought out new markets abroad, with the International Monetary Fund estimating that emerging and advanced Asian economies absorbed about half of the diverted trade, followed by the EU with near one-fifth.
After years of exporting disinflation to the rest of the world, higher input costs have led to an abrupt jump in Chinese export prices, with their gains accelerating in August to 15 per cent from a year earlier – the most since 2022.
The prices of imports surged even faster, however, and rose almost 30 per cent, the fastest increase in data going back two decades.
At the same time, businesses in China are struggling to pass on their growing raw material expenses to buyers, adding pressure on margins as industrial profits rise at the weakest pace this year. Despite a sharp upswing in producer inflation last month, the consumer price index (CPI) undershot estimates with an increase of 0.9 per cent, while the core CPI rose 1 per cent for a second straight month.
As domestic demand stagnates, the booming exports are also generating more pushback from China’s largest trade partners. After months of standoff with the EU, Brussels and Beijing have agreed to cap imports of hybrid cars from China, according to the bloc, though China describes the deal as ensuring “export space and steady growth” for its carmakers.
China reported a record trade surplus of US$34.8 billion with the EU in September, which was before the two sides announced the outcome of their talks. The imbalance was almost 21 per cent higher than in the same month a year ago.
The number of countries running trade deficits above 3 per cent of their gross domestic product with China more than tripled since 2005 to 82 last year, according to economists at Goldman Sachs Group, who estimate that most of them are low-income emerging economies.
Apart from the EU, Beijing’s other major trading partners saw unprecedented shipments from China last month in value terms. Record-high exports were bought by Australia, South Korea, Taiwan, Russia and the South-east Asian nations in the Asean group.
Sales to the US grew 40 per cent, the fastest in more than five years, as it ramps up purchases of capital goods needed for the buildout of AI infrastructure. That caused China’s trade surplus with the world’s biggest economy to swell to US$34 billion, the highest since January 2025. BLOOMBERG

Two key targets to focus on in the fourth quarter are total power generation capacity and the growth rate of B2C e-commerce. These are areas identified by the Ministry of Industry and Trade as requiring close monitoring and management to ensure the achievement of the 2026 targets. Currently, total power generation capacity stands at approximately 85,594.88 MW, requiring an additional 2,570.12 MW to reach the minimum scale of 88,165 MW by the end of the year. Meanwhile, the B2C e-commerce market grew by 19.5%, 0.5 percentage points lower than the lowest target of 20-22%.

Based on the performance results and the growth requirements for the whole year, the Ministry of Industry and Trade has identified a single operational scenario, aiming to achieve the 2026 targets, with a specific roadmap for October, November, and December. The results exceeding the schedule in the first nine months are considered a safe margin and will not be used to adjust the operational requirements downwards in the remaining months of the year.
For exports, the focus of management has shifted to maintaining a reasonable growth rate, improving the quality of growth, controlling the origin of goods, limiting trade risks, and reducing dependence on the foreign direct investment (FDI) sector.
A notable aspect of the new scenario is the application of a three-tiered risk management mechanism (green, yellow, and red) for each indicator on a monthly basis. When an indicator reaches the warning threshold, the lead unit must immediately activate the prepared solutions, without waiting for the quarterly assessment results. Importantly, an indicator must not remain at the Red level for more than one month without a solution being implemented and reported.
This approach shows that the operational requirements of the Ministry of Industry and Trade are shifting strongly from evaluating results to proactively identifying, preventing, and handling risks, closely monitoring actual developments to promptly adjust solutions.
Accelerate e-commerce, ensure power supply.
According to the updated scenario, the average Industrial Production Index (IIP) for the remaining months of the year is expected to reach approximately 12.5-13%, ensuring that the annual growth rate remains within the target range of 12-14%. Total electricity production and imports in the fourth quarter are estimated at approximately 88.55 billion kWh, bringing the total annual output to approximately 355.13 billion kWh, an increase of about 9.92%. Annual export turnover is expected to increase by approximately 22.8%, while total retail sales of goods and consumer service revenue are projected to increase by approximately 13.3%.
For B2C e-commerce, the projected growth rates for October, November, and December are 21%, 23%, and 26%, respectively, bringing the annual growth rate to approximately 20.5%. The percentage of businesses adopting e-commerce is expected to reach around 68%, approximately 6 percentage points higher than the upper limit of the target.
To realize these goals, the Ministry of Industry and Trade requests that efforts be made to maximize the year-end shopping peaks and the 2026 Online Friday shopping event; coordinate with major e-commerce platforms to implement programs promoting the consumption of Vietnamese goods, supporting shipping and payment costs. At the same time, it calls for promoting the listing of businesses, cooperatives, and OCOP products on these platforms, and expanding logistics and digital payment services in rural areas.
The Department of E-commerce has been tasked with shifting its focus from expanding the number of participants to increasing actual transactions. Key tasks include strengthening seller verification, ensuring transparency of product information, managing livestreaming activities, affiliate marketing, and cross-border e-commerce; and improving methods for measuring the size of the B2C e-commerce market, ensuring that the data accurately reflects reality.

For the electricity sector, the Ministry of Industry and Trade requires the creation of a list of contingency projects with a total capacity of no less than 120% of the remaining capacity shortfall, equivalent to approximately 3,100 MW. Along with this, it calls for accelerating the process of granting commercial operation certificates (COD) for each unit and each part of the project that meets the criteria; shortening the testing and acceptance time to bring power sources into operation as soon as possible.
In the domestic market sector, key tasks include implementing the second national concentrated promotional program, carrying out the "Vietnamese people prioritize using Vietnamese goods" campaign, proactively preparing goods for Tet (Lunar New Year), and implementing solutions to stabilize the market.
Regarding export activities, the Ministry of Industry and Trade focuses on controlling the origin of goods, improving the effectiveness of free trade agreements (FTAs), and expanding markets in the Middle East, Africa, Latin America, and Halal markets.
Updating growth scenarios on a monthly basis, linked to risk warning mechanisms and specific responsibilities of each unit, provides a foundation for the Ministry of Industry and Trade to proactively address bottlenecks, focus resources on challenging targets, and resolutely achieve the 2026 growth target and create a foundation for development in 2027.

articles.title: UOB raises Vietnam’s 2026 GDP growth forecast to 9.2% - Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.summary: UOB raises Vietnam’s 2026 GDP growth forecast to 9.2%  Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.full_text:
Ho Chi Minh City (VNA) – Singapore’s United Overseas Bank (UOB) has raised its forecast for Vietnam’s GDP growth in 2026 to 9.2% from 8.5%, following stronger-than-expected third-quarter performance and upward revisions to first-half figures.
However, the bank said the 10% growth target remained difficult to achieve, while rising inflation would complicate monetary policy management.
In its latest macroeconomic report, UOB also raised its 2027 growth forecast to 8.8% from 8.4%.
Vietnam’s GDP grew 9.95% year-on-year in the third quarter, bringing growth in the first nine months to 9.01%, above UOB’s forecast of 9% and the 8.65% Bloomberg consensus.
To achieve its full-year forecast, Vietnam would need fourth-quarter growth of around 9.7%, supported by year-end public investment disbursement, a seasonally strong export quarter, and record FDI inflows.
The official 10% target would require roughly 12.5–13% growth in Q4, and likely remains beyond reach, though 2026 growth is set to beat 2025's 8% by a clear margin, UOB said.
S&P Global’s manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) fell from 53.3 in August to 51.9 in September, while new export orders declined for a second consecutive month, at the fastest pace since April.
UOB’s upgraded 2027 forecast reflects expectations that registered FDI will increasingly translate into production capacity, alongside industrial upgrading and higher value manufacturing.
In the first nine months of 2026, registered FDI reached 50.36 billion USD, up 76.4% year-on-year, while disbursed FDI rose 12.1% to 21.07 billion USD.
Key risks include energy price spikes given the unresolved US-Iran conflict, possible tighter US tariffs following the 2026 midterm elections, power supply and other infrastructure constraints, and delays in public investment execution.
UOB also raised its average inflation forecast for 2026 to 4.7% from 4.1%. The consumer price index (CPI) increased 5.08% year-on-year in September, while average inflation in the first nine months reached 4.52%, exceeding the official target of 4.5%. The bank expects headline inflation to remain around 5% in the fourth quarter.
Above-target inflation, rapid credit growth and the prospect of further US Federal Reserve interest rate increases are complicating monetary policy management for the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV).
Yet tighter monetary policy may do little to curb largely supply-driven inflation pressures.
"We expect the SBV to hold the refinancing rate at 4.5% through 2027, relying on open market operations and credit-quota guidance, but see the risk now skewed towards a hike," UOB said./.

articles.title: UOB raises its forecast for Vietnam's GDP growth in 2026 to 9.2%. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: UOB raises its forecast for Vietnam's GDP growth in 2026 to 9.2%.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
UOB forecasts Vietnam's GDP growth in 2026 to reach 9.2%, along with forecasts of rising inflation and monetary policy challenges amidst better-than-expected growth.
Ahead of better-than-expected economic growth in the third quarter of 2026, on October 13th, the Global Market and Economic Research Department of UOB Bank ( Singapore ) raised its forecast for Vietnam's GDP growth for the whole year to 9.2%.
In addition, UOB raised its forecast for average inflation in 2026 from 4.1% to 4.7%, while maintaining its view that the State Bank of Vietnam will keep the policy interest rate unchanged amid increasing price pressures.
Growth exceeded expectations.
According to a report by UOB, Vietnam's economy continues to record positive results, with GDP in the third quarter of 2026 increasing by 9.95% year-on-year, exceeding Bloomberg's consensus forecast of 8.65% and the bank's earlier forecast of 9%.
This is the highest quarterly growth rate since Q3 2022. Notably, after the Q1 and Q2 growth figures were revised upwards to 8.15% and 8.81% respectively, Vietnam's economy has maintained its acceleration for three consecutive quarters.
Overall, GDP grew by 9.01% in the first nine months, significantly higher than the 7.8% growth rate for the same period in 2025. This result further strengthens Vietnam's position among the fastest-growing economies in the ASEAN region.
Looking at economic sectors, industry and construction continued to be the leading drivers with a 12.5% increase in the third quarter. The service sector grew by 9.54%, while agriculture, forestry, and fisheries increased by 4.21%.
Also during the past nine months, industry and construction increased by 11.21%, contributing nearly half of the total value-added growth of the economy. The service sector increased by 8.69%, contributing 45.03%.
According to UOB experts, growth is not only concentrated in major economic centers but also spreads to many localities, with 12 out of 34 provinces and cities achieving growth rates of 10% or more in the first nine months of the year.
The electronics sector continues to play a prominent role, with exports of computers, electronic products, and components reaching approximately US$111 billion by mid-September. UOB believes this result shows that Vietnam is benefiting from the global wave of investment in artificial intelligence (AI).
However, some indicators suggest a slowdown in the manufacturing outlook. The manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) fell from 53.3 points in August to 51.9 points in September, while new export orders declined for the second consecutive month.
In the investment sector, registered foreign direct investment (FDI) in the first nine months increased by 76.4%, reaching US$50.36 billion. Disbursed FDI reached US$21.07 billion, an increase of 12.1% and the highest level for the same period in the past five years.
Regarding public investment, by the end of August, the disbursement rate reached 50.5% of the annual plan. According to UOB, the remaining public investment capital in the record plan of VND 1.08 trillion will continue to create room to support growth in the final quarter of the year.
Inflationary pressures are increasing.
Alongside positive signs of growth, the UOB report also points out several challenges facing the Vietnamese economy, particularly the trade balance and inflation.
In September, exports increased by 39.1% year-on-year, reaching $59.48 billion, while imports increased by 45.8%, reaching $58.21 billion. As a result, the trade balance recorded a surplus of $1.27 billion, marking the first month of surplus after nine consecutive months of deficit.
You may also like
However, for the first nine months of the year, exports reached $434.30 billion, an increase of 24.5%, while imports reached $453.72 billion, an increase of 36.7%. The trade balance therefore showed a deficit of $19.42 billion, in contrast to a surplus of $16.87 billion in the same period last year.
UOB attributes the sharp increase in import value to energy prices. Notably, 94.1% of import value falls under the category of raw materials and inputs for production, indicating that import demand is primarily linked to the expansion of production activities.
The bank expects the trade balance to continue to record a surplus in the final months of the year thanks to the peak export season and lower energy prices. However, the trade balance for the whole year is likely to remain in deficit.
Regarding inflation, the consumer price index (CPI) in September rose 0.62% compared to the previous month and 5.08% year-on-year, higher than the 4.89% recorded in August.
The main upward pressure on prices comes from the transportation sector due to rising fuel prices, along with adjustments to tuition fees at the start of the new school year. Meanwhile, core inflation is at 4.45% year-on-year.
Overall, for the first nine months, the average CPI increased by 4.52%, slightly exceeding the target of 4.5%, while core inflation averaged 4.26%.
According to UOB, inflationary pressures remain in the final quarter of the year due to the ripple effect of rising energy prices, sustained strong domestic demand, and continued credit growth of around 16% year-on-year.
Based on this, UOB forecasts that CPI will remain around 5% in the fourth quarter, bringing the average inflation rate for the whole of 2026 to approximately 4.7%, higher than the previous forecast of 4.1%.
Raising GDP forecast to 9.2%, interest rates may remain unchanged.
Following better-than-expected growth results, UOB decided to raise its forecast for Vietnam's GDP growth in 2026 from 8.5% to 9.2%. This forecast implies growth in the fourth quarter reaching approximately 9.7%, supported by public investment disbursements, the peak export season, and positive FDI inflows.
However, to achieve its 10% growth target for the whole year, UOB estimates that the Vietnamese economy needs to grow by approximately 12.5%-13% in the final quarter of the year.
For 2027, UOB raised its GDP growth forecast from 8.4% to 8.8%, based on the expectation that registered FDI inflows will gradually translate into actual production capacity, along with reforms and the development of high value-added industries.
Alongside the positive outlook, UOB notes risks from energy price volatility, US tariff policies, electricity supply constraints, infrastructure, and the potential for delays in public investment disbursement.
Regarding monetary policy, UOB believes that the State Bank of Vietnam is facing the challenge of balancing support for growth and inflation control.
You may also like
Against the backdrop of inflation exceeding targets, credit growth outpacing deposit mobilization, and the Federal Reserve's projected continued interest rate hikes, pressure to tighten monetary policy is increasing.
However, UOB argues that raising interest rates may not be very effective in controlling inflation, as price pressures mainly come from the supply side, and it risks impacting growth momentum.
Therefore, this bank continues to forecast that the State Bank of Vietnam will maintain the refinancing interest rate at 4.5% until the end of 2027, while using open market tools and credit growth limits to regulate liquidity. However, the possibility of an interest rate increase is becoming a more significant risk.
Regarding exchange rates, UOB stated that the Vietnamese Dong had appreciated by approximately 1% year-to-date as of October 2nd, trading around 25,987 VND/USD.
According to UOB's forecast, the USD/VND exchange rate could be at 26,300 VND in Q4 2026, rising to 26,600 VND in Q1 2027 and 26,800 VND in Q2-Q3 2027.
UOB assesses that positive FDI inflows, GDP growth prospects above 9%, and the potential for an improved trade balance will continue to support the stability of the Vietnamese dong, despite continued pressure from the Fed's interest rate policy and volatility in international capital flows.
Overall, UOB believes that the Vietnamese economy is maintaining strong growth momentum, but inflationary pressures and external uncertainties will place increasingly demanding requirements on monetary policy management in the coming period.

articles.title: S&I Ratings: Q3 GDP growth surges to 9.95%, but key drivers lag behind. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: S&I Ratings: Q3 GDP growth surges to 9.95%, but key drivers lag behind.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
S&I Ratings assesses that Vietnam's economy will experience breakthrough growth in the third quarter of 2026 amidst tightening global financial conditions. GDP in the third quarter increased by 9.95%, bringing the nine-month growth to 9.01%, but the main drivers remain industry, exports, and investment, while domestic consumption is recovering more slowly.
Industry and exports became the main driving force.
According to S&I Ratings' Q3 macroeconomic report, Vietnam's GDP in Q3 2026 is estimated to have increased by 9.95% year-on-year, higher than the 8.15% growth in Q1 and 8.81% in Q2. The growth rate continues to improve quarter by quarter, indicating a positive trend for the economy.
Overall, GDP grew by 9.01% year-on-year for the first nine months. This is the highest growth rate in many years, excluding 2022, when growth was particularly impacted by the recovery from the Covid-19 pandemic. However, S&I Ratings noted that the growth structure still shows significant differences between sectors. Industry and construction contributed more than half of the overall growth, while domestic consumption and the service sector have not recovered proportionally.
According to this organization's assessment, the economy is still operating primarily based on external drivers such as exports, FDI, and infrastructure investment, rather than domestic demand. In the first nine months, the industrial and construction sector grew by 11.21%, significantly exceeding the 8.69% growth of the service sector and the 4.02% growth of the agriculture, forestry, and fisheries sector.
Khám phá thêm
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch
Khám phá ĐNA
Compared to the 8.69% growth in the first nine months of 2025, the industrial and construction sector has accelerated significantly this year. This growth is driven by all three main groups: manufacturing (up 11.36%), construction (up 12.22%), and electricity and gas production and distribution (up 10.62%). This upward trend is also reflected in the Industrial Production Index (IIP), which increased by 16.7% in September and 12.3% over the nine months.
Several sectors recorded strong growth in September, including metal ore mining (up 58.1%), beverage production (up 24.7%), metal manufacturing (up 21.8%), and electronics and computer manufacturing (up 23.3%).
According to S&I Ratings, the manufacturing sector is being supported by two main drivers. First, exports of computers, electronics, and technology are surging thanks to a wave of global investment in AI, data centers, and semiconductors. Second, demand for construction materials and electricity is increasing along with the progress of large-scale infrastructure projects domestically, thereby supporting the steel, cement, and energy sectors.
Exports accelerate, trade balance returns to surplus.
A notable development in September was the 39.1% increase in exports compared to the same period last year, reaching nearly $60 billion, a record high. Thanks to exports keeping pace with import growth, the trade balance after nine months returned to a surplus of $1.27 billion, after a period of consecutive deficits.
You may also like
S&I Ratings believes that the accumulated volume of imported raw materials from the beginning of the year is gradually being converted into export volume in the final months of the year. Exports also tend to accelerate as the year-end peak season approaches. However, the strong increase in export value is not only due to increased production but also influenced by commodity prices, especially the rising price of electronic components amidst a global chip shortage.
Cumulatively from the beginning of the year, exports increased by 24.5%, while imports increased by a staggering 36.7%, resulting in a trade deficit of $19.42 billion. By product category, computers continued to be the biggest driver. Exports of this item in September increased by 112.7% year-on-year, accounting for 38% of total export value and contributing 72% to the overall export growth. Many basic industrial product groups also showed positive growth, such as iron and steel (up 55.7%), chemicals (up 68.6%), electrical wires (up 42.1%), and transportation equipment (up 21.9%). Conversely, some agricultural products experienced slow growth, or even negative growth, such as rice, vegetables, and cashew nuts.
Public investment continues to play a leading role.
Investment activity maintained a positive trend and continued to play a crucial role in economic growth. Public investment disbursement in September increased by 58% compared to August. For the first nine months of the year, the total disbursed value reached VND 642.9 trillion, completing 62.9% of the plan and increasing by 12.9% compared to the same period last year.
Excluding the 5% of local government budget allocated for public investment savings to fund the Lao Cai - Hanoi - Hai Phong railway line, the implementation rate reached 64.8%. Given the slow recovery of domestic consumption and the volatile external environment, S&I Ratings believes that public investment continues to be a driving force for growth.
The significantly improved disbursement rate in the third quarter not only created a ripple effect on the construction and materials industries but also boosted credit demand, employment, and private investment through large-scale infrastructure projects. Alongside public investment, FDI inflows continued to record positive results. Actual FDI increased by approximately 12.1% in the first nine months of the year, while newly registered and supplementary FDI increased sharply by 76.4% year-on-year.
Inflation exceeds 5%, narrowing the scope for further monetary easing.
High economic growth is accompanied by increasing inflationary pressure. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) in September rose 5.08% year-on-year, mainly due to an 11.67% increase in transportation costs driven by international energy prices. S&I Ratings suggests that the sharp rise in global oil prices amid escalating geopolitical tensions in the Middle East is one of the factors putting pressure on transportation costs.
You may also like
On the positive side, most other commodity groups tended to cool down, with food and education prices easing pressure. Core inflation in September decreased slightly to 4.45%. For the first nine months, inflation averaged 4.52%, close to the government's inflation control target of 4.5%.
Nevertheless, rising transportation and energy costs could directly impact domestic production and purchasing power. The CPI exceeding 5% also indicates that the room for maintaining loose monetary policy is narrowing.
According to S&I Ratings, if oil prices continue to remain high, inflationary pressures could become more pronounced, especially in the context of an economy experiencing near-double-digit growth.
Consumer spending is recovering but has not yet achieved a breakthrough.
In contrast to the strong growth in production and exports, domestic consumption has recovered relatively slowly. For the first nine months of the year, total retail sales of goods and consumer service revenue increased by approximately 13.4% year-on-year. After excluding price factors, the actual increase reached about 7.8%. S&I Ratings assesses that consumer trends continue to improve compared to the same period last year, but the recovery rate is significantly slower than that of the manufacturing and export sectors.
This indicates that Vietnam's economic growth in the first nine months of the year still relies heavily on the export-oriented manufacturing sector rather than domestic demand. In this context, the challenge for the economy in the remaining months of the year lies not only in maintaining high growth momentum, but also in strengthening domestic demand while controlling inflationary pressures and adapting to a still-tight global financial environment.

articles.title: GDP growth may exceed 4.5%-5.5% forecast on tech and construction gains - Singapore Business Review
articles.summary: GDP growth may exceed 4.5%-5.5% forecast on tech and construction gains  Singapore Business Review
articles.full_text:
The forecast comes despite economic growth easing to 5.4% in Q3 from 6.2% in Q2.
Singapore's economic growth could exceed the government's 2026 forecast range of 4.5% to 5.5%, as strong electronics exports and construction activity helped drive growth to an average of about 6% in the first three quarters, according to eToro.
"For the year to stay inside that range, it means the fourth quarter (Q4) would have to stop growing altogether, which is unlikely to happen," said Zavier Wong, market analyst at eToro.
He further expects the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry to lift its 2026 GDP growth forecast next month.
Wong’s assessment followed GDP expansion of 5.4% year-on-year in Q3, moderating from an upwardly revised 6.2% in the previous quarter.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore said in its October Macroeconomic Review that the economy is expected to continue expanding steadily in the coming quarters, with the artificial intelligence (AI)-led expansion remaining relatively well-anchored into 2027.
Separately, United Overseas Bank (UOB) raised its full-year growth forecast to 5.7% from 5.0%, citing upward revisions to first-half growth and stronger-than-expected Q3 performance.
The bank said that wholesale and retail trade, alongside transportation and storage, rose 2.2% quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) on a seasonally adjusted basis, compared with flat growth in Q2.
UOB attributed the improvement partly to stronger wholesale trade activity involving machinery, equipment and supplies, supported by demand related to AI.
Construction also rebounded by 3.4% QoQ, reversing a 2.7% contraction in Q2, whilst manufacturing declined 0.9% following a 6.3% expansion.
However, the bank expects GDP growth to moderate to 3.2% in 2027 due to higher comparison bases and an anticipated slowdown in AI-related investment.
It also warned that higher global interest rates could weigh on consumption and non-AI investment in Singapore's major trading partners, potentially affecting external demand.
Meanwhile, RHB maintained its 2026 growth forecast at 5.0%, with upside risks towards 5.4%.
The bank expects electronics and precision engineering to continue supporting manufacturing growth through the remainder of the year, driven by demand for AI infrastructure and semiconductors.
Electronics output grew 27.1% year-to-date, whilst precision engineering expanded 16.3%, it said.
RHB also highlighted construction as the fastest-growing sector in Q3. It expects major infrastructure projects, including Changi Airport Terminal 5, Cross Island Line Phase 2 and Tuas Port, to sustain construction activity.
The bank also maintained its industrial production and non-oil domestic export growth forecasts at 9.0% and 15.5%, respectively.
However, Wong warned that economic growth remains uneven, with most gains coming from electronics exports and construction rather than household spending.
"Most households aren't seeing that growth in their wallets," he said.
RHB similarly cautioned that weaker wage growth, cautious hiring and higher transportation costs could weigh on discretionary spending and retail activity in the second half of the year.
The bank also identified uncertainty over US tariffs and a potential slowdown in AI-related investment as risks to Singapore's manufacturing and export outlook.

articles.title: Guangxi eyes stronger marine economy, deepens ASEAN ties - China Daily
articles.summary: Guangxi eyes stronger marine economy, deepens ASEAN ties  China Daily
articles.full_text:
South China's Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region is accelerating the high-quality development of its marine economy and leveraging major infrastructure projects to deepen international trade cooperation, particularly with Southeast Asian nations, officials said.
The region has witnessed robust growth in both its maritime sectors and overall foreign trade. During the first half of this year, Guangxi's marine gross product reached 137.7 billion yuan ($20.57 billion), marking a 6.8 percent year-on-year increase driven by advances in marine engineering equipment, offshore wind power and marine fisheries. This upward trajectory continued into the broader trade sector, with total foreign trade volume from January to August growing by 9.6 percent to 567.23 billion yuan.
Lin Zenan, deputy director of Guangxi's Development and Reform Commission, noted that the region is actively optimizing its industrial layout along coastal areas, transportation corridors and inland waterways to build a modernized marine industrial system.
Central to this economic transformation is the enhancement of maritime and inland connectivity. Beibu Gulf Port, a crucial international gateway, handled 312 million metric tons of cargo and 6.189 million twenty-foot equivalent units of containers in the first eight months of the year.
Furthermore, the economic belt surrounding the newly operational Pinglu Canal generated a regional GDP of 712.63 billion yuan in the first half of the year, up 3.7 percent year-on-year.
Lin emphasized that Guangxi is upgrading its infrastructure network, including railways and port facilities, to seamlessly integrate port operations with industrial and urban development, ultimately transforming port cities into highly livable and business-friendly hubs.
Guangxi's strategic location has solidified its role as a vital hub for trade with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, which has maintained its position as Guangxi's largest trading partner for 26 consecutive years. From January to August, bilateral trade reached 284.69 billion yuan.
Wang Xinhong, deputy director of the China (Guangxi) Pilot Free Trade Zone office, highlighted the region's success in creating a highly efficient supply chain for agricultural products. During the same period, Guangxi imported 30.45 billion yuan worth of fruits from ASEAN, accounting for more than one-third of the national total, with half of all durians imported into China passing through Guangxi ports.
Additionally, the region is securing cross-border industrial supply chains, with intermediate goods trade surging by 18.5 percent to reach 410.09 billion yuan, ensuring stable manufacturing operations across the border.
The China (Guangxi) Pilot Free Trade Zone has played a pivotal role in driving institutional openness and attracting global capital. During the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021-25) period, the region utilized $7.36 billion in actual foreign investment. Wang pointed out that the free trade zone is pioneering cross-border innovations, including the establishment of an artificial intelligence development path tailored for ASEAN applications, supported by AI cooperation agreements signed with eight ASEAN member states.
The zone is also fostering a robust marine wind power industrial cluster. As the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 approaches implementation, local authorities are further streamlining cross-border data flows and expanding service trade in digital and cultural sectors.
Meanwhile, local authorities are committed to balancing economic expansion with rigorous ecological security. Lin said Guangxi is implementing comprehensive environmental protection measures for coastal wetlands and mangroves, and has successfully promoted its marine ecological restoration experience nationwide. By prioritizing both technological innovation and green development, the region aims to ensure that its pursuit of a strong marine economy remains highly sustainable.

By REN QI in Liuzhou, Guangxi | China Daily | Updated: 2026-10-16 09:47
Liuzhou Railway Vocational Technical College is ramping up its global outreach by tailoring vocational training programs to support the expansion of Chinese manufacturing and infrastructure enterprises across Southeast Asia, officials said.
Located in the industrial hub of Liuzhou, Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, the college has focused its educational resources on five ASEAN member states — Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Laos and Vietnam. Over the past five years, the institution has trained more than 1,200 international students and provided over 25,000 days of technical training for overseas Chinese companies.
To ensure practical proficiency, the campus features a massive outdoor railway training field equipped with active enterprise machinery, as well as simulated driving laboratories that replicate the exact CR200J train models used in international infrastructure projects.
A flagship example of this initiative is the college's deep involvement in Malaysia's East Coast Rail Link project. Wang Hanqiang, Party secretary of the college, said the institution collaborated with project developers to compile a comprehensive operation and maintenance management system. This partnership generated millions of words of maintenance standards and dozens of technical regulations tailored specifically to Malaysia's railway conditions and local laws.
Wang said this approach ensures technical standards are effectively adapted to local contexts rather than merely exported. Furthermore, similar railway occupational standards developed by the college have recently been incorporated into the national vocational standards of Laos.
To bridge cultural and technical gaps, the college employs a customized educational model designed to prevent a disconnection between classroom learning and practical application. Wang mentioned that students are often selected by partner enterprises before enrollment, allowing them to sign employment contracts in advance. Their curriculum seamlessly combines language studies, classroom instruction and on-site project internships.
This customized approach also resonates on a personal level. For instance, the college is currently training several Lao students in railway operations after they were inspired to enroll after seeing their older siblings successfully secure technical roles on the China-Laos Railway following their graduation from the same institution. Consequently, over 200 international students enrolled in these customized railway classes have already secured technical positions, providing overseas projects with a steady stream of skilled local workers.
Beyond railway transportation, the college is aligning its programs with the booming new energy vehicle sector. Partnering with local automotive giant SAIC-GM-Wuling, the school has established specialized training bases to cultivate technicians for Southeast Asia. Thai and Indonesian students receive hands-on experience in battery testing and vehicle maintenance. Many of these students transition directly into employment at the automaker's overseas branches upon graduation, while the college has also successfully trained dozens of master-level technicians specifically for the Indonesian automotive market.
Such efforts reflect a broader strategy within Liuzhou to integrate vocational education with industrial development. Zhao Congkui, deputy director of the Liuzhou Municipal Education Bureau, said the city's vocational programs are designed to strictly follow industrial layouts. With over 90 percent of local vocational majors matching key regional industries, the city ensures that its talent supply meets precise market demand. Zhao pointed out that this integration is now backed by local legislation, marking a shift toward legally guaranteed industry-education cooperation.
In addition, local institutions have helped establish 19 overseas training centers and multiple modern artisan academies across ASEAN countries, Zhao added.
Looking ahead, Zhao said that the city plans to build a unified international brand for its vocational education, cultivate bilingual teaching staff and establish additional cross-border platforms. Furthermore, as the region develops the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, Liuzhou will expand its curricula to include multimodal transport, ensuring a continuous supply of talent for broader international logistics networks.

By Manoj Kumar
NEW DELHI, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Canada is racing to seal a trade pact with India and deepen ties with the European Union as it seeks to reduce reliance on the US amid President Donald Trump's protectionist trade policy, Foreign Minister Anita Anand said on Wednesday.
The push is central to Prime Minister Mark Carney's plan to diversify trade and strengthen ties with the EU, China and other countries even as Ottawa seeks to maintain cooperation with Washington on trade, defence and security.
"The Comprehensive Economic Partnership agreement with India is part of our trade diversification strategy, and yes, we aim to conclude it by the end of the year," Anand told Reuters in an interview at the Canadian High Commission in New Delhi.
"Canada has a goal of doubling non-US trade over the next 10 years," Anand said.
Canada and the EU are expected to discuss cooperation on critical minerals, energy and artificial intelligence at a summit later this month, building on trade ties under the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), Anand said.
Canada is also broadening its trade partnerships, having signed a free trade agreement with Indonesia last year and is looking to sign a pact with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in 2026. Ottawa has concluded 15 trade agreements covering 51 countries and 1.5 billion consumers, she said.
"It is really about our national resilience and our sovereignty," Anand said. "We need to ensure that we are not reliant on any one country for the economic resilience that our country has been able to exhibit."
INDIA TRADE PACT
Negotiations on the India agreement were progressing well, Anand said, adding that Indian trade negotiators had visited Canada last week and Canadian Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu was in India with a business delegation.
Carney and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi had discussed the agreement, she said. Modi is expected to visit Canada in December.
Canada says a deal could more than double bilateral goods and services trade to $70 billion annually by 2030 from the $30.4 billion recorded in 2025. Goods trade with India reached $10.9 billion in 2025, with Canadian exports falling 26.5% from 2024, while imports from India rose by 18.9%.
A C$2.6 billion ($1.8 billion) uranium supply agreement between Canadian company Cameco and India, signed earlier this year, was one tangible outcome of closer cooperation, she said.
In one example of deepening economic ties, Canada's Fairfax Financial Holdings has agreed to buy a majority stake in India's IDBI Bank in a deal valued at 528.78 billion rupees ($5.56 billion), in what will be India's biggest cross-border bank deal.
