Hanoi (VNA) – A series of major events aimed at promoting bilateral economic and trade cooperation took place in Hanoi on October 14, including the ninth Vietnam-US Business Summit and a seminar entitled “The US Market in 2026: Opportunities, challenges and breakthrough solutions”.
The events were jointly organised by the American Chamber of Commerce in Vietnam (AmCham) and the Vietnam Chamber of Commerce and Industry (VCCI), highlighting a shift in foreign investment towards high technology and the urgent need for Vietnamese businesses to ensure supply chain transparency when accessing the US market.
Addressing the summit, Permanent Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc said economic ties have entered a new era of growth more than three years after the establishment of the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.
Despite global uncertainty, Vietnam’s economy grew 9.01% in the first nine months of 2026, attracted more than 50 billion USD in registered foreign direct investment (FDI), and recorded 888 billion USD in trade turnover.
However, Vietnam’s development orientation will undergo a fundamental shift, he said. In line with Resolution No. 10-NQ/TW, the country will move away from attracting individual investment projects towards developing investment platforms centred on industrial clusters and innovation ecosystems.
Future Vietnam-US cooperation will prioritise semiconductors and artificial intelligence, clean energy, sustainable supply chains, innovation, and high-quality human resources training.
To achieve these goals, the Government is committed to accelerating institutional reforms, removing infrastructure bottlenecks, and adopting a more development-enabling approach, the Deputy PM said, calling on the US to ensure objective and balanced assessments in trade investigations and to conclude negotiations on a reciprocal trade agreement soon, helping Vietnamese goods gain stable access to the US market.
At the seminar, VCCI Vice Chairman Hoang Quang Phong urged domestic businesses to move beyond exporting raw materials and minimally processed products, build their own brands and increase their participation in higher value-added stages of production.
Tran Thanh Hai, Deputy Director of the Agency of Foreign Trade under the Ministry of Industry and Trade, identified five pillars shaping US trade policy, namely reciprocity, trade balance, economic security, domestic manufacturing promotion and supply chain security.
Against this backdrop, transparency in the origin of raw materials has become critical. Vietnamese businesses that remain confined to basic processing and assembly will find it increasingly difficult to withstand increasingly sophisticated technical barriers.
Former Vietnamese Trade Counsellor in the US An The Dung warned that policy changes, product quality issues and legal disputes have posed risks to exporters, despite bilateral trade having increased nearly 300-fold over the past 30 years.
He urged businesses to assess policy risks, strengthen their capacity to protect their interests and tighten control over production processes, particularly in sensitive areas such as food safety and hygiene.
Proactive information disclosure, standardised management procedures and improved product quality will help Vietnamese goods expand their presence and establish a lasting foothold in the US market, he added./.

articles.title: How DBS, OCBC and UOB Are Betting on AI in 2026 - Fintech Singapore
articles.summary: How DBS, OCBC and UOB Are Betting on AI in 2026  Fintech Singapore
articles.full_text:
What happens when artificial intelligence stops being an experiment and starts becoming part of how a bank actually works?
Singapore’s three largest homegrown banks, DBS, OCBC and UOB, are already well into that transition, with each reporting more than 300 AI use cases.
Each has disclosed a different mix of results this year, which becomes clearer when looking at what each bank has put into production and where the impact is already measurable.
DBS says it runs more than 430 AI use cases, and OCBC and UOB each put theirs at more than 300.
Every bank counts in its own way, and UOB’s figure includes analytics, so the totals only go so far.
A better test is what each bank has put in front of its bankers and customers this year, and what it can show for it.
DBS Puts Numbers on Its AI Push
DBS has put hard numbers on its AI work.
Its 2025 annual report counts more than 430 use cases across over 2,000 AI models and estimates that its data analytics and AI and machine-learning initiatives delivered about S$1 billion in economic value in 2025.
The newer effort is agentic AI, software that carries out a chain of tasks instead of answering a single question.
In August, DBS gave around 1,500 relationship and credit risk managers worldwide a tool that works through more than 70 such tasks to draft a corporate credit memo, the document that makes the case for lending to a company.
It grew out of a pilot with 150 staff, and bankers and credit risk managers still make the assessment and approval decisions.
Customers are meeting the same technology in chat.
Late July saw DBS said its DBS Joy and digibot assistants, which now carry generative and agentic AI features, serve more than 10 million customers across Singapore, Hong Kong and Taiwan.
Some of those features let users finish a banking task without leaving the conversation.
Ahead of its March AGM, DBS told shareholders in written answers that it is redesigning processes, expanding collaboration between employees and AI, and reskilling staff as part of changes to its operating model.
OCBC’s Most Visible AI Launches This Year Are in Wealth
OCBC’s 2024 annual report counts more than 300 AI use cases, though its most prominent 2026 launches have centred on wealth management.
OCBC WoW, launched on 1 July, is built around two AI avatars, Wendy and Wayne, which clients can talk or type to about their portfolios using answers drawn from OCBC’s investment research.
The beta is open to staff and invited Premier Private Client customers with at least S$1.5 million in assets under management.
Bank of Singapore followed later that month with HELIOS, an agentic AI platform that handles much of the information gathering and due diligence before a relationship manager takes on a new client.
OCBC is targeting a median of 15 business days to open a private banking account, compared with an industry median of about six weeks, provided clients submit their documents promptly.
HELIOS builds on Bank of Singapore’s Source of Wealth Assistant, launched in October 2025 to draft reports tracing a client’s source of wealth.
Once documents are uploaded, the tool cuts preparation time from 10 days to one hour, and relationship managers review the draft before it is finalised.
The bank also uses AI to train its wealth advisors.
Participants in a six-month GenAI programme for 900 Singapore advisors booked twice as many weekly client appointments as untrained peers, Computer Weekly reported.
OCBC also reported a 50% revenue uplift against their previous three months, although both figures came from early in the programme.
Beyond wealth management, CFOtech reported in 2025 that the bank screens payments for scams in under 15 milliseconds, while an Asian Banker award write-up said personalised engagement drove 40% of sales.
UOB’s Clearest Published AI Results Come From Risk Management
More than 300 AI and analytics use cases are now in production at UOB, one of its executives said, as QA Financial reported.
An August investor presentation shows where they are heading, from wealth advisory in private banking to contact centres and software development.
It also describes a programme called AURA that is building agentic AI for anti-money laundering and know-your-customer checks, credit, collections and relationship manager support.
The same deck says more than 35,000 staff have been enabled with Microsoft Copilot, and UOB says it has built more than 30 domain-specific chatbots on its Build-Your-Own-Bot platform.
The hardest numbers come from risk.
Project Magnet, a surveillance tool in UOB Private Bank that pairs machine learning with rules-based checks, has raised true hits, the alerts that turn out to be genuine risks, by 148% and improved exception rates by 130%, UOB reports.
In commercial banking, B-Score 2.0 draws on more than 3,100 data points to spot early signs that a borrower is struggling to repay, The Digital Banker wrote.
Customers meet UOB’s AI as well.
Through the TMRW app, the bank served close to 180 million personalised insight cards to more than 2.5 million customers in 2023, per a Cloudera case study, and it runs a model that predicts wait times at its branches.
MAS Has Issued Its Final AI Risk Guidelines
The rules are now final.
On 7 October, MAS issued its Guidelines on AI Risk Management for all regulated financial institutions, which take effect on 7 October 2027, with some requirements phased in until October 2028.
MAS also plans to consult the industry in 2027 on whether agentic AI needs further guidance, OpenGov Asia reported.
The guidelines follow a busy year for the regulator, which finished the second phase of Project MindForge in March and published an AI Risk Management Toolkit built with 24 financial institutions and other industry partners.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and industry partners introduced the SAFR framework for agentic finance in July, and an AI-focused cyber and technology risk task force followed with the Association of Banks in Singapore later that month.
Back in August, MAS announced S$220 million over three years under FSTI 4.0, which includes support for wider AI adoption in financial services.
Speaking at a DBS event in May, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said slowing AI adoption would weaken Singapore’s competitiveness, while urging companies to think about what new roles could be created and how existing workers could be retrained.
From October 2027 onwards, the banks’ AI deployments will fall under those supervisory expectations.

Laos is working to strengthen economic ties with Azerbaijan, including by coordinating a bilateral investment agreement, Lao Deputy Minister of Industry and Commerce Manothong Vongsay said at the Azerbaijan-Laos Business Forum in Baku on Wednesday, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.
"Laos could serve as a gateway to Asian markets, particularly Southeast Asia, for Azerbaijani companies. Developing transport and logistics links between the two countries could create new opportunities to facilitate trade and expand economic cooperation," he said.
He said the forum provides a valuable opportunity for business communities from both countries to exchange information on economic policies, investment opportunities, and potential areas of cooperation, as well as to establish long-term business partnerships.

Vongsay emphasized that one of Laos’ main economic objectives is to transform the country from a landlocked nation into a regional transport and logistics hub, strengthen connections between markets, and facilitate the movement of goods and people.
“This strategy is aligned with regional connectivity projects, including China’s Belt and Road Initiative. The Laos-China Railway plays an important role in implementing this strategy. In addition to providing passenger and freight services between Laos and China, the railway strengthens links with neighboring countries and regional markets,” he said.
The deputy minister noted that the Lao government is also expanding domestic infrastructure and cross-border connectivity. In this context, the government has decided to implement a railway project linking the Lao capital, Vientiane, with Vietnam. The Vientiane-Hanoi highway project is also intended to strengthen Laos’ links with Vietnam’s port infrastructure.
“I believe Laos can serve as an important gateway for Azerbaijani businesses seeking access to Asian markets. Vongsay identified mining, agriculture, energy, transport, and logistics as promising areas for cooperation between the two countries. He also highlighted opportunities to promote investment in green steel production projects with commercial potential and viable project structures.
The deputy minister also outlined measures to improve Laos’ investment climate. He said the government amended the Law on Investment Promotion in 2024 and is considering further improvements to the legal framework in 2026, including the introduction of additional incentives, to attract more foreign direct investment.
According to Vongsay, in addition to the 22 special economic zones already operating in Laos, two industrial parks have been established to attract investment and support industrial development.
“These areas offer investment opportunities and incentives in manufacturing, digital technologies, research and development, data centers, and agricultural processing. The government is expanding digital public services to improve the business environment. Online payment options for import duties and taxes, as well as foreign currency services through the banking system, are being developed to simplify business operations and reduce the administrative burden,” he said.
The deputy minister noted that investment activity in Laos has shown positive momentum despite complexities in the global and regional economic environment. Approximately $16 billion in investment was approved during the five years from 2021 through 2025.
He added that 24 investment projects worth approximately $8.5 billion were approved in the first seven months of 2026, representing a 68% increase compared with the same period last year.

“Nevertheless, there is significant potential for the two countries to work together in several areas,” he said.

articles.title: Singapore growth to stay firm, but AI boost to moderate in 2027: MAS - The Business Times
articles.summary: Singapore growth to stay firm, but AI boost to moderate in 2027: MAS  The Business Times
articles.full_text:
Core inflation is expected to ease from mid-2027
[SINGAPORE] The Republic’s economy is expected to continue expanding in the quarters ahead, though the pace of artificial intelligence-related activity is projected to moderate in the latter half of 2027.
In the near term, strong orders for AI products and an increase in production capacity “should sustain firm growth in the technology-related sectors”, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said in its macroeconomic review on Wednesday (Oct 14).
The review was released after advance estimates from the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry showed that Singapore’s economy grew 5.4 per cent year on year in the third quarter.
MAS also kept its Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate policy settings unchanged on Wednesday, against private-sector economists’ expectations, after two consecutive tightenings earlier this year.
The central bank said in its review that core inflation is expected to “ease more discernibly” from the middle of 2027, but risks remain tilted to the upside. Inflation could rise more than anticipated if renewed disruptions in the Middle East trigger another surge in energy prices, or adverse weather leads to larger increases in food prices.
AI’s impact on growth
MAS said Singapore’s economy is “expanding at an above-trend pace”, with technology-related sectors supporting firm gross domestic product growth in Q3.
Strong order backlogs and capacity expansions in AI-related production should sustain growth in the near term, it said. The global AI investment cycle is expected to remain a key growth support, even as AI-driven growth moderates from its exceptional pace.
In Singapore, AI-related activity is projected to moderate in the latter half of 2027, while construction and financial services activity continue apace.
Computing and data-centre demand is expected to rise through 2027, lifting capital expenditure expectations for US hyperscalers. Semiconductor production is also expected to remain elevated in the coming quarters and could rise further as new capacity comes on stream.
The risks of an AI cycle downturn “appear less immediate”, MAS said. “A materially weaker growth outcome would likely require a financial shock that emanates from a sharp reassessment of expected returns across the AI ecosystem,” it added.
One plausible scenario is an “AI infrastructure credit shock”, in which weaker-than-expected AI monetisation leads hyperscalers to cut capital expenditure and prompts a repricing of debt-financed AI investments.
This could tighten financial conditions, delay projects across the AI supply chain and trigger a self-reinforcing downturn in investment and global growth.
Inflation remains elevated in the near term
MAS expects Singapore’s core inflation to “remain slightly elevated in the immediate quarters ahead”, before easing more discernibly from mid-2027.
It forecasts core and headline inflation to average 1.5 to 2.5 per cent in 2027. For 2026, it expects core inflation to average 1.5 to 2 per cent and headline inflation around 2 per cent.
Core inflation rose to 2.1 per cent year on year in July and August, from 1.5 per cent in the second quarter.
MAS attributed the increase to earlier rises in energy and other imported costs filtering through to electricity and gas, food, and fuel-intensive services such as airfares and point-to-point transport.
Enhanced healthcare subsidies and larger discounts on telecommunications services partly offset the increases by lowering prices in those categories.
“Taken together, price increases in the economy broadened but at a relatively gradual pace,” MAS said.
Imported inflation is expected to stay elevated in the near term.
Brent crude and refined fuel prices have risen anew amid renewed conflict in the Middle East and are expected to remain high in the coming months, before easing over 2027 as oil and gas flows normalise.
El Nino-related weather disruptions could push up food prices, though healthy inventories in major producing countries should limit the increase.
MAS expects the impact on Singapore’s food prices to fade in the latter part of 2027 as the weather-related shocks dissipate.
Globally, the economy has remained resilient despite the energy shock, supported by the technology upcycle. Alternative supplies, inventory drawdowns, softer oil demand and fiscal subsidies have helped cushion the impact of disrupted energy flows.
Lower-than-expected inflation readings prompted MAS to lower its global inflation forecasts to 2.5 per cent for 2026 and 2 per cent for 2027, from 2.7 and 2.2 per cent, respectively, in its July review.
But global headline inflation is expected to edge up in the coming months as higher energy costs continue to reach consumers.
MAS estimates that up to a third of the energy shock has yet to feed through to consumer prices; inflation should then ease gradually in 2027.
For Singapore, MAS said tighter global financial conditions could weigh on growth and inflation, while a faster resumption of crude and distillate shipments from the Middle East could cause inflation to fall more quickly than expected.
Labour market
MAS said Singapore’s labour market conditions remain stable: Vacancies still outnumber unemployed persons and resident unemployment remains low, although retrenchments have risen.
Wage growth is expected to moderate to around historical norms, while unit labour cost growth should remain subdued amid firm productivity gains.
Construction and domestic-oriented services are expected to support hiring, though resident employment growth will slow as labour supply expands more slowly with an ageing population.

articles.title: Indonesia Targets Year-End Finish for Landmark EU Trade Pact as Business Lobby Urges Global Push - InvestorTrust
articles.summary: Indonesia Targets Year-End Finish for Landmark EU Trade Pact as Business Lobby Urges Global Push  InvestorTrust
articles.full_text:
Indonesia Targets Year-End Finish for Landmark EU Trade Pact as Business Lobby Urges Global Push
Key Takeaways
| ● | Indonesia and the European Union are pushing to conclude and ratify the long-awaited I-EU CEPA trade pact before the end of 2026. | 
| ● | Indonesian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (Kadin) Chairman Anindya Bakrie called on domestic exporters to aggressively prepare for expansion across European markets. | 
| ● | Priority export lines expected to gain broader preferential access include footwear, textiles and garments, furniture, electronics, processed foods, and coffee. | 
| ● | Indonesian Ambassador to the EU Andy Rachmianto highlighted that the pact is critical for leveling the playing field with regional peers like Vietnam and Singapore. | 
JAKARTA, Investortrust.id — Indonesia is racing to cross the finish line on its long-negotiated trade pact with the European Union by the end of 2026, prompting the country’s top business lobby to urge domestic exporters to prepare for an aggressive European market push.
Speaking after a closed-door consultation with Indonesian Ambassador to Belgium, Luxembourg, and the European Union Andy Rachmianto at the Kadin headquarters in South Jakarta on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, Kadin Chairman Anindya Novyan Bakrie said domestic industries must be ready to seize immediate export opportunities once the deal is cleared.
"Hopefully, the ratification of the I-EU CEPA trade agreement with the European Union will be up and running before the end of this year," Anindya said. "The Ambassador highlighted the uphill battle required to reach this stage, as well as the massive economic impact this will deliver for Indonesia's trade balance."
Confronted by rising global trade headwinds and an urgent need to diversify export destinations beyond traditional buyers, Southeast Asia's largest economy is betting that preferential access to the 27-nation European bloc will revitalize factory order books. For nearly a decade, Indonesian manufacturers have faced steep tariff disadvantages in Europe compared to regional competitors such as Vietnam and Singapore, which already operate under operational free-trade pacts with Brussels. Finalizing the agreement provides an essential springboard to scale value-added industrial shipments and attract premium European direct investment.
Unlocking High-Margin Export Corridors
Anindya emphasized that dismantling bilateral trade barriers will widen market access across several of Indonesia’s most competitive non-commodity export sectors. Key industries positioned for immediate upside include footwear, textiles and garments, furniture, electronics, processed food lines, and specialty coffee.
Those product lines already form the backbone of Indonesia’s manufacturing exports into advanced markets such as the United States. Gaining equivalent, duty-free entry into Europe opens an expansive parallel consumer base with significant purchasing power.
"These happen to be the exact same powerhouse sectors that we ship to markets like the United States," Anindya noted. "Opening up a broader market for essentially the same product categories represents a monumental commercial opportunity."
Leveling the Regional Playing Field
Indonesian Ambassador Andy Rachmianto underscored that strong institutional backing from Kadin and the domestic private sector is paramount to ensure the agreement translates into real commercial contracts rather than remaining paper commitments.
The European single market commands enormous consumer demand, and securing streamlined access will enable Indonesian commodities and processed goods to gain durable market share.
"Our shared hope is that, just as our ASEAN peers like Singapore and Vietnam have demonstrated, this CEPA agreement will serve as the primary growth engine for our export products entering European nations," Andy said.

Finance, information and communications, and professional services also continued to expand at a solid pace, but consumer-facing and other domestic services lagged.

articles.title: Thailand's next growth phase hinges on skills and structural reform - Nation Thailand
articles.summary: Thailand's next growth phase hinges on skills and structural reform  Nation Thailand
articles.full_text:
Thailand’s next phase of economic growth will depend on higher productivity, skilled workers and sustained structural reform rather than continued reliance on cheap labour and traditional manufacturing alone, senior policymakers and economists told a seminar in Bangkok on Tuesday (October 13).
Speaking at “Bangkok 1991–2026: Thailand’s Path to Resilient, Inclusive Growth”, held during the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Annual Meetings at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center, the speakers examined how Thailand transformed its economy, the lessons of the 1997 financial crisis and the structural challenges it must overcome to achieve stronger growth.
Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas traced Thailand’s first economic transformation to shifts in global manufacturing during the 1980s. Following the Plaza Accord and the appreciation of the yen, Japanese companies relocated production to Southeast Asia, helping Thailand attract foreign direct investment to its Eastern Seaboard, particularly into the automotive and electronics industries in Rayong.
Industrial expansion created factory employment, lifted incomes and helped reduce poverty from nearly 50% to below 5%, according to Ekniti. Yet annual growth of 8–10% concealed vulnerabilities, with excessive foreign-currency borrowing through the Bangkok International Banking Facilities contributing to the 1997 financial crisis.
Thailand subsequently strengthened its banking system and accumulated foreign reserves now worth nearly three times its short-term external debt. That stability, Ekniti argued, provides a foundation for growth but is insufficient without further economic transformation.
“Today, as noted, we face a rapidly ageing population and labour constraints. Therefore, our next economic takeoff cannot rely on cheap labour. We must focus on labour productivity, accelerating digital technologies, and cultivating human capital.”
With multinational companies diversifying production through a “China Plus One” strategy and Thailand seeing a surge in applications to the Board of Investment, Ekniti called for a second wave of high-technology investment, stronger links between Thai small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and global supply chains, and greater foreign participation in the services sector to encourage competition and technology transfer.
The government’s “Skill Bridge” programme connects international investors with Thai universities to jointly develop curricula and upgrade local engineers’ skills in electronics, semiconductors and artificial intelligence (AI).
Ekniti also highlighted a “Regulatory Guillotine” to remove outdated business restrictions and simplify digital work permit and visa approvals. Industrial development, he added, should spread beyond traditional centres to electronics in Lamphun, automotive components in Nakhon Ratchasima and semiconductor assembly in Songkhla, while maintaining fiscal discipline.
Bank of Thailand Governor Vitai Ratanakorn described the 1997 crisis as a turning point that prompted a managed-float exchange rate, flexible inflation targeting and stronger foreign reserves. Despite healthier bank capital and liquidity, Thailand’s underlying growth rate has steadily weakened.
Vitai traced the decline in Thailand’s trend growth from more than 7% before 1997 to around 5.3% after the crisis, 3.5% following the global financial crisis and about 2.4% since the pandemic. He projected economic growth of 2.1–2.3% in 2026, attributing the slowdown chiefly to structural rather than temporary problems.
“Fiscal policy should focus on targeted, supply-side structural investments and support for vulnerable segments, while monetary policy maintains price stability and ensures adequate macroeconomic policy space to cushion future external shocks.”
He stressed that closer coordination between fiscal and monetary policies must preserve central bank independence and fiscal credibility. Household debt and financing difficulties for smaller businesses were among the most pressing constraints.
According to figures he cited, lending to major corporations rose by 6%, while SME lending contracted for 16 consecutive quarters, falling 4.4% year on year. Credit remained relatively accessible to the top 30% of productive SMEs, he explained, but less productive businesses, particularly those operating with outdated business models, faced greater difficulties.
Rather than providing blanket subsidised loans, Vitai favoured targeted restructuring and support for technology adoption among viable SMEs in food processing, wellness and smart electronics, alongside orderly resolution for those unlikely to recover.
He also identified green finance, action against financial fraud and the use of AI to improve productivity as priorities.
Suthiphand Chirathivat, professor emeritus of economics at Chulalongkorn University, identified regional integration, adaptability and institutional capability as the foundations of Thailand’s next economic transformation.
He noted that regional trade was equivalent to nearly 90% of the gross domestic product (GDP) of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). The bloc also attracted US$243.9 billion in foreign direct investment in 2025, accounting for approximately 15% of global inflows.
“However, Thailand has struggled to capture its proportional share of these new investment waves compared to neighbours like Vietnam, Malaysia, and Singapore.”
“We cannot afford domestic complacency; Thailand must position itself as an indispensable node within regional value chains.”
Thailand also needed to adapt its established automotive industry to electric vehicles, batteries, semiconductors and embedded software while responding to the green transition and changes in global supply chains.
Citing an Asian Development Bank study, Suthiphand warned that nearly 80 million ASEAN workers could face disruption from generative AI, while the green transition could create 30 million jobs in the region by 2030.
“To capture these opportunities, Thailand must invest aggressively in workforce capability, curriculum reform, and institutional governance. We have excellent national master plans, but our implementation capability has historically been our weakest link.”
He warned that reforms often lose momentum across electoral cycles and that poorly managed technological change could widen income inequality and the digital divide between large companies and smaller businesses. Lifelong learning, flexible reskilling schemes, vocational training and public-private partnerships would be essential to help workers and smaller firms benefit from technological change rather than fall further behind.
Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF’s Asia and Pacific Department, placed Thailand’s experience within Asia’s wider rise.
Asia now accounts for about 60% of global GDP growth, compared with less than 25% three decades ago, Srinivasan noted. Over that period, Thailand’s GDP per capita increased from approximately US1,800tomorethanUS8,000.
He highlighted how the IMF had expanded its policy toolkit following the 1997 Asian financial crisis, including the Financial Sector Assessment Program to evaluate financial resilience and the more recent Integrated Policy Framework to help countries manage volatile capital flows.
With international capital becoming more selective, Srinivasan warned that economic progress alone would not guarantee future investment. He identified predictable policymaking, regulatory transparency and fiscal credibility as crucial factors influencing investors’ decisions.
He also highlighted the opportunities and employment challenges arising from AI adoption.
“IMF research across Asia shows that in sectors heavily exposed to AI, net labour demand initially dips by approximately ten per cent. However, labour demand subsequently stabilises because AI augments tasks rather than eliminating entire occupations.”
Broad access to AI tools, continuous training and education reform would therefore be necessary to turn automation into more inclusive productivity gains.
The speakers agreed that Thailand’s stronger financial foundations provide an important starting point, but sustained growth will require more effective reforms, higher productivity and a skilled workforce capable of turning new technologies and foreign investment into opportunities for domestic businesses and workers.

articles.title: On the eve of VIS 2026: Vietnam's opportunities amidst new trends in the global economy. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: On the eve of VIS 2026: Vietnam's opportunities amidst new trends in the global economy.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Capital flows are becoming more selective. Technology is restructuring industries and value chains. New demands for quality, sustainable development, and adaptability are reshaping the rules of the game. As the global economy enters a profound reshaping cycle, Vietnam's opportunities lie not only in its ability to attract shifting capital flows, technologies, and supply chains, but also in its capacity to transform these flows into new productivity, knowledge, and value for the economy.
An open economy is situated amidst major currents.
The global economy in 2026 is caught between two opposing forces. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecasts world economic growth of around 3% in 2026, lower than the average of 3.5% in 2024–2025. But behind this relatively stable growth rate lies an increasingly clear divergence: geopolitical instability is putting pressure on many economies, while the technology investment cycle, particularly around artificial intelligence, is strongly boosting countries already deeply involved in the global technology value chain.
International capital flows paint a similar picture. According to UNCTAD, global foreign direct investment is projected to recover by 6% in 2025, reaching approximately $1.6 trillion, after two years of decline. However, the recovery is highly uneven across different groups of economies.
These figures reflect a more significant shift: global resources are still flowing, but increasingly tend to gravitate towards places capable of absorbing, connecting with, and creating value from them. This is where Vietnam's position becomes particularly noteworthy.
Vietnam is entering this transitional cycle with a high-growth economy and deep integration with international trade and investment. By 2025, Vietnam's GDP is projected to grow by 8%. Exports are expected to increase by 16.7%, while disbursed FDI is projected to reach US$27.6 billion, a 9% increase year-on-year, amidst the continued restructuring of regional value chains.
The latest forecasts for 2026 continue to show the maturity of the economy. In September, the ADB raised its growth forecast for Vietnam to 7.8%, while the World Bank in early October raised its forecast to 7.4%, partly due to high-tech manufacturing and exports benefiting from the global technology cycle.
On another note, Vietnam currently ranks 43rd out of 139 economies in the Global Innovation Index 2026. Notably, Vietnam ranks 35th in innovation output but 54th in innovation input, demonstrating a relatively good ability to generate results from existing resources, while also revealing significant room for growth in human resources, research, institutions, and the necessary foundations for innovation to occur on a higher scale.
Based on this data, Vietnam is in a unique position: open enough to benefit significantly from new economic flows, but also integrated enough into the global economy that continuous capacity building becomes a necessity.
Therefore, the question for the next phase is no longer simply how much more investment, factories, or technology Vietnam can attract. More importantly: how much capacity will these flows leave behind for the Vietnamese economy?
When innovation is no longer limited to technology.
You may also like
In many discussions, innovation is often directly linked to artificial intelligence, semiconductors, startups, or the latest technologies.
But the nature of innovation is much broader. According to the OECD approach, innovation is not just an invention or a new idea. An idea only becomes innovative when it is put into use and creates real change. Innovation can be in the product, but it can also be in the production process, logistics, management, organizational methods, or how a business interacts with external partners.
In that sense, innovation is first and foremost the ability to see a problem from a different perspective, and then to organize resources to transform that perspective into new value. This could be innovation in policy thinking, when a city designs new institutional models to compete for capital and talent. It could be innovation in businesses, when technology is not simply acquired, but entails changes in processes, management, and supply chain organization. It could be innovation in universities, when research goes beyond scientific publication and can reach the market. It could be innovation in the relationship between corporations and startups, when a business does not just seek an existing product but brings its real-world problem outside the organization to jointly develop a solution. Or it could be a shift in thinking about sustainable development, when green standards, energy efficiency, and traceability are no longer considered merely compliance costs, but become part of competitiveness.
Technology can make those processes happen faster. Standards can help new values be measured, trusted, and scaled up. But the starting point still lies in the ability to re-examine and find a better way to solve existing problems. That's also why innovation is increasingly seen not as an independent field, but as a class of capabilities permeating the economy.
VIS 2026 and the question of a "breakthrough point" for Vietnam.
In this context, the Vietnam Innovation Summit (VIS) 2026 has chosen the theme “Critical Mass – The New Currents of Innovation: Vietnam at the Center of a Global Realignment”.
"Critical Mass" can be understood as the point at which individual elements converge to a sufficient degree to create change. In an economy, this breakthrough is unlikely to come from the number of startups, investment capital, or new technologies alone. It occurs when capital, knowledge, technology, businesses, institutions, and people begin to interact strongly enough for individual changes to connect, spread, and create ecosystem-wide capabilities.
The VIS 2026 framework is built on that very logic. This year's Vietnam Innovation Summit series begins with a discussion about Free Trade Zones, International Financial Centers, and Vietnam's future investment attraction, followed by deep technology and future industries, while also bringing universities into discussions about knowledge transfer, research commercialization, and the role of collaboration models between the state, businesses, and universities.
This year, the conference also dedicated significant space to dialogue on a broader level: What capabilities will Vietnam use to compete when its traditional advantages are no longer sufficiently differentiating? The program ranges from competition through benchmarking, open innovation and collaboration between corporations and startups to green economy, energy transition, and ASEAN investment connectivity.
In the forum "Competing by Setting Standards in the Era of Economic Shift," this question was broadened through a dialogue between regulatory agencies, international organizations, financial experts, and businesses. With the participation of representatives from the Ho Chi Minh City Department of Industry and Trade, the ASEAN- Switzerland Chamber of Commerce, the Vietnam International Finance Centre, and Masterise Group, the discussion not only addressed how businesses need to raise their standards, but also went further to the conditions under which these capabilities can be formed and scaled up: from the institutional environment and market dynamics to the long-term investment choices of the businesses themselves. This is also how VIS approaches the story of innovation on a broader scale: not viewing individual changes as isolated phenomena, but placing them within the relationship between policy, market, businesses, and the capabilities that the economy needs to build for the next phase.
From seizing opportunities to creating capabilities
How can Vietnam transform the opportunities presented to it in its economy into capabilities that belong to it? This is not only a central issue raised at VIS 2026, but also a question that economists, businesses, and experts are constantly pondering in the era of economic pivot.
You may also like
An economy can grow by absorbing external capital, technology, and demand. But long-term competitiveness depends on whether those resources generate new productivity, knowledge, businesses, and capabilities domestically.
The World Bank believes that the ability to retain more value domestically, increase linkages between foreign-invested and domestic enterprises, and improve productivity will be crucial to the medium-term strength of the Vietnamese economy.
Viewed in that light, innovation should not be understood as an “industry.” It is a method of development. When a business finds a more efficient way of operating, that is innovation. When a university transforms knowledge into a product that solves a societal problem, that is innovation. When institutions create a new structure to facilitate the easier flow of capital, talent, and technology, that is also innovation. And when an economy is able to transform these individual innovations into an ecosystem that can continuously learn, experiment, collaborate, and upgrade itself, innovation begins to become a national competitive advantage.
This is also the role that VIS 2026 aims for: not to find a single technology or a single solution, but to create a space where stakeholders holding different parts of the solution can meet, from policymakers, businesses, investors to universities, startups and international partners. The VIS component is designed to span from government and diplomatic agencies to businesses, financial institutions and investment funds.
In a world where economic flows are constantly reshaping, Vietnam's position will therefore not be determined solely by what is moving into Vietnam. More importantly, it will depend on what Vietnam does with those flows, what capabilities it creates from them, and what role it plays in shaping subsequent flows.

articles.title: IMF warns of widening economic gaps amid an AI investment boom - Nation Thailand
articles.summary: IMF warns of widening economic gaps amid an AI investment boom  Nation Thailand
articles.full_text:
Global economic growth may hold at 3.1% in 2026, but that resilience rests on increasingly fragile foundations as investment in artificial intelligence (AI) drives uneven growth and governments confront high debt, inflation and rising energy costs, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned.
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva gave the warning at the “Debate on the Global Economy: Forging Resilient and Dynamic Economies for the Future” during the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Thursday (October 15).
She was joined by senior economic policymakers from Thailand, Greece, Argentina and Nigeria.
“So, yes, growth has been resilient. But this resilience is on a fragile foundation today,” Georgieva told the discussion. The IMF’s projection for 2026 remained at 3.1%, the same as its estimates in October 2025 and April 2026.
She highlighted widening differences between economies benefiting from AI and those hit by war or rising fuel costs. The United States, China and India were among the AI producers, while Thailand and South Korea benefited through their links to AI supply chains, she added.
Rising energy and food prices, potentially exacerbated by El Niño, could keep inflation elevated, prompting central banks to tighten monetary policy and pushing up debt-servicing costs. AI investment had become a crucial source of growth, raising the risk of disruption if expectations proved unrealistic or AI systems operating beyond human control threatened financial stability.
“We have a world economy that is like on one leg. The rest of the economy not so strong. What happens if this leg wobbles?” Georgieva asked.
She called on governments to rebuild policy buffers and reduce debt. She also warned of persistent economic imbalances, citing China’s weak domestic consumption and heavy exports, insufficient saving and large deficits in the United States, and inadequate investment and productivity growth in parts of Europe.
Despite these challenges, Georgieva expressed greater optimism than a year earlier that excessive global economic imbalances could be resolved.
Thailand’s Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas likened the country to a small boat navigating four storms: higher energy prices, geoeconomic fragmentation, rising borrowing costs and the disruptive spread of AI.
Oil imports raised Thailand’s living costs, while supply-chain diversification opened investment opportunities. Ekniti put Thailand’s 10-year government bond yield at around 2.3%, below those of the United States and Europe, crediting fiscal discipline and macroeconomic stability.
Yet stability alone was insufficient, he argued. The government also needed to help low-income households and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) adapt to technological change and participate in new supply chains, rather than allow economic inequalities to widen.
“Building resilience is to support them to absorb the shocks, and also to accelerate the transitions to help them deal with bigger storms coming,” Ekniti told the panel.
He called for deeper regional integration, noting that trade within ASEAN accounted for about 22% of the region’s total trade, compared with around 60% for trade within the European Union. He cited the ASEAN Power Grid, which could help countries share hydropower from Laos and reduce their exposure to energy shocks.
Ekniti also backed ASEAN’s Digital Economy Framework Agreement, closer links between national digital identification systems and cross-border QR payments connecting Thailand with Singapore and Malaysia. Thailand was also negotiating a free-trade agreement with the European Union, he added.
On investment, Ekniti reported that foreign direct investment applications in the first half of 2026 had increased by 47% to approximately US$44 billion. He highlighted opportunities in AI, smart electronics and electric vehicles, while private investment had grown by more than 10% for two consecutive quarters.
He outlined the Skill Bridge programme, designed to connect foreign investors with Thai universities and SMEs, transfer knowledge and strengthen local participation in global supply chains. Simplifying investment approvals and removing bureaucratic obstacles were also priorities.
Ekniti compared new investment opportunities to high-speed trains arriving in Thailand, with Thai people and businesses waiting on the platform.
“We [are] trying to open more doors for Thai people, Thai businesses, to go into the speed train and then use [those] opportunities to upgrade Thai productivity,” he said.
Kyriakos Pierrakakis, president of the Eurogroup and Greece’s minister of economy and finance, described Europe as “mindful, but not alarmed” about rising bond yields. He cited a rise in average 10-year bond yields from 1.1% in 2016 to around 4% in 2026, making fiscal credibility more important. Greece’s experience, he argued, showed why discipline and structural reform had to advance together.
“The markets are looking at your fiscal trajectory. And especially in a high-yield environment, they’re looking at it much more acutely,” he explained.
Pierrakakis identified productivity as Europe’s biggest challenge, contrasting average annual productivity growth of 1.8% in the United States with 1.1% in Europe over three decades. He advocated banking integration, stronger capital markets and larger cross-border businesses, arguing that internal fragmentation restricted growth.
He pointed to the Savings and Investment Union, which combines capital market and banking reforms. Citing IMF estimates, he likened internal European barriers to tariffs of 110% on services and 40% on manufacturing, and urged faster action to remove them.
Argentina and Nigeria draw on crisis reforms
Argentina’s Economy Minister Luis Caputo cautioned that resilience could disappear quickly if a major country encountered financial trouble. He defended President Javier Milei’s policies, reporting a 30% reduction in government spending, the elimination of the fiscal deficit and a decline in inflation from 211% in 2023 to around 30%.
“We do not need the whole world to collapse. Just one country, one important country getting into trouble could generate a systemic risk and affect all of us,” Caputo warned.
Caputo also credited reforms with creating more than 500,000 jobs and reducing poverty from 57% to 32%. He projected around US$200 billion in investment under Argentina’s Incentive Regime for Large Investments (RIGI) over the coming years and identified food, energy and critical minerals as sectors offering further opportunities.
Nigeria’s central bank governor, Olayemi Cardoso, described how monetary tightening, foreign exchange reforms and greater transparency had helped restore confidence after a currency crisis. The central bank raised rates by around 800 basis points in 2024, he noted, while inflation subsequently eased from about 34% to 15% and reserves reached their highest level in 18 years.
Cardoso also pointed to the removal of costly subsidies and the unification of multiple exchange rates. He highlighted the Dangote refinery as a means of adding value to Nigeria’s oil production.
He also reported clearing more than US$7 billion in overdue foreign-exchange obligations. Easier remittance transfers had helped raise monthly inflows from roughly US$200 million to US$600 million, reaching about US$950 million by July.
“We were able to do the right things through an orthodox monetary policy approach, which helped to stabilise the economy. We were, believe it or not, able to pay off those debts, and we were able to attract investment,” he explained.
Across the discussion, speakers highlighted a common challenge: resilience depends not only on withstanding shocks but also on credible policies, institutional reform and measures that help businesses and workers benefit from economic change.

articles.title: Chairman of Ho Chi Minh City: We must accelerate in the fourth quarter to boost annual growth to 10.2%. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Chairman of Ho Chi Minh City: We must accelerate in the fourth quarter to boost annual growth to 10.2%.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
On the morning of October 15th, Ho Chi Minh City held a conference to review the socio-economic development situation in the first nine months of 2026, focusing on promoting double-digit economic growth, implementing investment projects, and stimulating demand.
Attending the conference were the Secretary of the Ho Chi Minh City Party Committee, Tran Luu Quang ; the Deputy Secretary of the City Party Committee and Chairman of the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee, Nguyen Van Duoc; the Deputy Secretary of the Ho Chi Minh City Party Committee, Dang Minh Thong; leaders of the Ho Chi Minh City People's Council and People's Committee, along with relevant units and localities.
Fourth quarter growth must reach 13.23%.
According to a report by the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee, the estimated GRDP for the first nine months of the year reached 2.46 trillion VND. The 9.06% growth rate is the highest in the last 10 years. However, this result is still 0.37 percentage points lower than the projected growth scenario for the first nine months.
Regarding attracting foreign direct investment (FDI), in the first nine months of 2026, Ho Chi Minh City achieved $17.8 billion, 4.2 times higher than the same period last year. Within the economic sectors, agriculture, forestry, and fisheries increased by 3.12%, exceeding the projected 3.05%. Industry and construction increased by 9.18%, lower than the targeted 9.86%. Services increased by 9.27%, lower than the projected 9.63%.
Five sectors achieved or exceeded the targets: transportation and warehousing; information and communication; arts, entertainment and recreation; finance, banking and insurance; and other service activities.
Conversely, nine sectors did not meet their targets, including wholesale and retail trade (up 8.2%), accommodation and food services (up 5.28%), and real estate business (up 4.82%).
To achieve an annual growth rate of 10.2%, the GRDP for the fourth quarter must increase by 13.23%. The Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee has requested a review of industries, projects, works, and production and business activities that have the potential to generate additional growth in the last three months of the year.
Ho Chi Minh City aims to accelerate the commencement of key investment projects and construction works, removing obstacles related to procedures, land, premises, capital, and labor to enable businesses to expand production, increase capacity, orders, and product consumption.
Simultaneously, efforts should be made to boost year-end consumer demand through promotional programs, trade fairs, exhibitions, connecting supply and demand, attracting more tourists , and promoting trade to expand export markets.
According to Hoang Vu Thanh, Director of the Ho Chi Minh City Department of Finance, a major task for the city in the final quarter is the disbursement of public investment funds. After nine months, the disbursement rate reached 75.5% of the capital plan assigned by the Prime Minister .
The city aims to disburse 100% of the planned budget, prioritizing key transportation projects, urban infrastructure, flood control, urban beautification, healthcare, education , and projects that contribute to growth.
You may also like
In the first nine months, total budget revenue reached approximately 82.4% of the projected amount, but only about 67% of the target of 1 trillion VND.
Ho Chi Minh City is calling for increased revenue from land, combating revenue losses in e-commerce, digital platform businesses, real estate, and other sectors with a high risk of revenue loss. It will continue to address obstacles related to land, planning, construction, and site clearance; and accelerate projects outside the budget, stalled projects, and land areas with the potential to generate revenue.
Simultaneously, the city will implement the Urban Development Law, finalize the city's master plan for the period 2025-2050, with a 100-year vision, in October 2026, and accelerate urban railway projects, TOD planning, and social housing development.
Accelerate progress on key projects.
In his opening remarks at the conference, Chairman of the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee Nguyen Van Duoc stated that although many positive results have been achieved, the current growth rate has not yet reached the planned target, creating significant pressure for the final quarter of the year. In particular, disbursing public investment funds in the last three months of the year is a crucial task, requiring units to focus on handling numerous issues.
At the same time, we urge corporations, businesses, and investors to accelerate investment progress, contributing to the overall growth of the city. Simultaneously, departments, agencies, and localities need to focus on removing obstacles for key projects and large-scale projects, creating favorable conditions for investors to implement their projects.
The Chairman of the People's Committee of Ho Chi Minh City emphasized that the city's public investment disbursement target for 2026 must reach 100%. For projects where obstacles have been removed, the city aims for over 50% of projects to become operational, exploited, and used in practice… to generate revenue and growth.
Departments, agencies, and localities need to focus on resolving issues with a positive and highly responsible spirit, accelerating the progress of handling projects by private investors, and contributing to improving the city's investment environment.
At the conference, Chairman Nguyen Van Duoc requested that departments and units present their information concisely, focusing on the issues that need to be addressed during the working sessions and coordinating the handling of tasks.
"The city will reward collectives, individuals, units, and localities with achievements in disbursement and land clearance work to encourage and motivate units that perform well, ensuring a spirit of fair rewards and punishments," Mr. Duoc said.

articles.summary: KPay Granted Major Payment Institution License by MAS  Fintech Singapore
articles.full_text:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has granted KPay a Major Payment Institution (MPI) license.
The license, held by subsidiary KPay Merchant Service (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. under the Payment Services Act 2019, authorises KPay to provide merchant acquisition, domestic money transfer and cross-border money transfer services in Singapore.
MAS gave KPay in-principle approval for the license in July 2026, subject to the company meeting specified conditions.
KPay set up its Singapore operations in 2022 and now serves more than 10,000 local merchants, mostly in the F&B and retail sectors.
The company said it has invested in governance, risk management, compliance, technology and operations to run a regulated payments business at scale.
For those merchants, KPay will now provide acquiring and money transfer services as a licensed MPI while it widens its product range.
Online payments and a POS system for F&B
KPay is adding Online Payments to its existing in-store payment acceptance services. The new offering supports e-commerce transactions, digital invoicing and remote payment collection.
The company is also launching KPay POS, an integrated point of sale system for Singapore’s F&B sector. It combines payment acceptance, inventory management and real-time business insights in one platform.
Both products are designed to help merchants manage payments and operations across physical and digital channels. They are also expected to extend KPay’s reach to new merchant segments.
“A restaurant owner should be able to accept an online order as effortlessly as a walk-in, and focus on what matters most: delivering a great dining experience,”
said Keith Chen, General Manager of Singapore, KPay Group.
“A retailer should have their payments and business data all in one place.”
KPay’s existing Singapore offering includes a unified merchant dashboard, real-time transaction analytics and single-source business data, supported by 24/7 customer response, dedicated account managers and on-site technical deployment.
The KPay MPI license and Singapore’s role in its expansion
Singapore is one of KPay Group’s two headquarters.
The company said it will use the standards developed for its Singapore business to support expansion across APAC, adapting them to each market’s legal and regulatory requirements.
“Our ambition is to build a connected ecosystem that supports merchants in how they accept payments and run their businesses, whether online or in-store,”
said Davis Chan, Chief Executive Officer, KPay Group.
“Singapore will remain a key market for that development and an important hub for the capabilities that support KPay’s continued growth across Asia-Pacific.”
KPay said it plans to keep growing its Singapore team and service capabilities as the business scales.

articles.title: From India, another example of incentives linked to investment performance. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: From India, another example of incentives linked to investment performance.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
In the context of increasingly fierce competition to attract foreign investment, India is linking incentives to revenue, domestic supply chains, and R&D activities. This approach is noteworthy as Vietnam is also refining its investment incentive and support policies to better align with project performance.
India is spending $7.5 billion, but not just to produce more phones.
On August 21, 2026, India announced the Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme 2026 (MPMS), following the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme which ended on March 31.
During the four years of implementing the PLI (Private Partnership in the Mobile Industry), from 2022 to 2025, India's smartphone exports increased more than sevenfold, from $3.1 billion to $24.1 billion. By 2025, smartphones will become the country's largest export item. This result lays the foundation for India to move to the next phase in its mobile phone industry development strategy.
Instead of focusing solely on expanding manufacturing and assembly, India aims to become a global mobile phone manufacturing and export hub, while also integrating the domestic supply chain more deeply into the process. The MPMS (Mobile Manufacturing and Production Management System) is designed to link the growth of production and revenue for businesses with the use of domestically sourced components as well as design, research, and development (R&D) activities.
A notable aspect of MPMS is that support is determined based on the actual performance of the business. For large-scale manufacturers, the support amount is calculated based on the portion of revenue exceeding the standard revenue threshold. Businesses that reach a certain revenue threshold and continue to maintain growth will be eligible for support.
This mechanism also encourages businesses to increase their use of components sourced from the Indian market. Phones using domestically sourced components can receive an additional subsidy of up to 1.5%. These components include screens, cameras, phone casings, batteries, and charging cables.
Indian domestic brands are eligible for higher levels of support if they meet conditions regarding ownership structure, operational control, and intellectual property rights, while also establishing design and research centers within the country. Thus, the level of support depends not only on size and revenue growth but also on the extent of participation in the domestic supply chain, as well as design and R&D activities.
You may also like
To implement the MPMS, India has allocated 62,500 crore rupees, equivalent to approximately US$7.5 billion. The program spans five fiscal years, from 2026-2027 to 2030-2031, with grants determined based on business performance.
The design of the MPMS shows that India is not simply allocating resources to increase mobile phone production. By linking support levels to business results and specific business activities, the program simultaneously aims at three goals: expanding revenue, increasing the use of domestically sourced components, and bringing more design and R&D activities into India.
This also marks a shift after the PLI phase. While the previous phase contributed to the rapid expansion of smartphone production and exports, MPMS places greater emphasis on value creation and retention within the economy , through domestic supply chains and higher-tech activities.
What are the implications for Vietnam?
India's approach to linking support resources to business performance is particularly noteworthy in the context of increasing competition for investment among Asian economies, while Vietnam is also refining its investment incentive and support policies in line with Resolution No. 10-NQ/TW dated June 8, 2026, of the Politburo on the development of the foreign-invested economy.
In a recent report, the Foreign Investment Agency of the Ministry of Finance noted that regional economies such as India, Malaysia , and Thailand are stepping up incentive packages to attract shifting capital flows, especially in strategic sectors like semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI), data centers, and renewable energy. This creates additional competitive pressure on Vietnam in attracting and retaining high-quality investment projects.
At the same time, the need to innovate the methods of investment incentives and support has been raised. Resolution 10 emphasizes the need to "gradually shift from traditional incentives to a support mechanism linked to the operational efficiency of projects."
You may also like
One of the tools Vietnam is using is the Investment Support Fund, established under Decree No. 182/2024/ND-CP. The fund aims to stabilize the investment environment; encourage and attract strategic investors and multinational corporations; and support domestic businesses in certain sectors requiring investment incentives. Businesses meeting the eligibility criteria can receive support for costs such as training, R&D, fixed asset investment, and the production of high-tech products.
The Investment Support Fund is designed for multiple sectors, rather than focusing on a specific industry like the MPMS. This difference highlights a noteworthy aspect of resource allocation. With the MPMS, India selects a specific industry, clearly defining desired outcomes, from revenue growth and domestic supply chain development to bringing design and R&D activities domestically, and then links support levels to each of those outcomes.
In the context of limited support resources and increasingly fierce competition for investment, the selection of priority sectors and the level of resource concentration have become crucial factors in policy design and implementation. Focusing more on a few industries and sectors with the potential to create high added value, form supply chains, and disseminate technology can help support resources have a more significant impact, rather than allocating them too broadly.
Besides leveraging the effectiveness of the Investment Support Fund under Decree 182 to retain investors and supply chains, in the face of fierce competition to attract investment, India's method of quantifying results to determine the level of support in the MPMS program provides valuable experience for Vietnam as it gradually shifts from traditional incentives to performance-based support mechanisms in the future.

articles.full_text:
Union Minister for Finance and Corporate Affairs Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman concluded her official visit to Singapore from October 8 to 11, 2026, after a series of high-level bilateral engagements and meetings with leading global investors, financial institutions and businesses aimed at strengthening India–Singapore economic and financial cooperation.
During the visit, the Union Finance Minister called on H.E. Mr. Tharman Shanmugaratnam, President of Singapore, and H.E. Mr. Lawrence Wong, Prime Minister of Singapore, and met H.E. Mr. Gan Kim Yong, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade & Industry, and H.E. Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan, Minister for Foreign Affairs.
The engagements provided an opportunity to review progress in advancing the outcomes of the 4th India–Singapore Ministerial Roundtable (ISMR) and explore avenues to further deepen the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. The two sides also exchanged views on strengthening India–ASEAN cooperation and regional economic ties, including in the run-up to Singapore’s ASEAN Chairmanship in 2027.
Smt. Sitharaman also participated in a luncheon meeting hosted by H.E. Mr. Tharman Shanmugaratnam, President of Singapore, and Ms. Kristalina Georgieva, Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF). The luncheon brought together senior leaders from global financial institutions, investment firms, academia and the Singapore Government, providing an opportunity for exchanges on global economic and financial developments.
Discussions with Singapore’s leadership focused on expanding bilateral investment, strengthening financial connectivity and advancing cooperation in emerging technologies. The Union Finance Minister highlighted India’s strong macroeconomic fundamentals, growth prospects and ongoing policy reforms, and encouraged greater investment by Singapore-based institutional investors and businesses in India’s growth story. Select infrastructure projects from the National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF) pipeline were highlighted for consideration by investors, with a view to facilitating follow-up discussions and engagement with relevant Indian authorities.
As part of the investment outreach, Union Minister for Finance and Corporate Affairs Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman participated in a business roundtable with senior representatives of leading global financial institutions and investment firms, including JPMorgan Chase, BlackRock, Deutsche Bank, PIMCO, the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA), Carlyle, Temasek, Millennium Management, Citadel, and Brevan Howard. The discussions covered India’s continued commitment to economic reforms and resultant economic resilience amidst global uncertainties, developments in global and domestic financial markets, the implications of rapid advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), and opportunities to attract greater global capital into Indian assets. The participants expressed confidence in India’s growth story. They remarked that they look forward to continued progressive, fiscally prudent, predictable, growth-oriented policies of the government along with a focus on infrastructure.
The Union Finance Minister also held separate bilateral meetings with senior leadership of major institutional investors, financial institutions, and global corporations, including Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (MUFG), Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC), Wellington Management, Standard Chartered Bank, GIC (Government of Singapore Investment Corporation), DBS Bank, Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken (SEB), Temasek, TPG, HPS Investment Partners, CapitaLand Investment, Intel, British International Investment (BII), IHH Healthcare, and B Capital.
The senior leadership of these financial institutions and global corporations expressed strong investment interest in key sectors, including consumer markets, start-ups, FinTech, Deep-tech, and healthcare. These engagements also explored investment and financing opportunities across infrastructure, especially AI and AI related infrastructure including semiconductors and data centres, renewable energy for India’s energy transition and energy security, manufacturing, MSMEs and trade finance, financial services, food supply chains and other growth-oriented sectors.
Opportunities relating to aircraft leasing, treasury centres and greater participation by global investors in India’s financial markets were also explored. Mobilising long-term institutional capital and expanding avenues for financing India’s infrastructure and development priorities were key themes of the investment discussions. Smt. Sitharaman encouraged investors to explore opportunities through the NIIF and GIFT International Financial Services Centre (GIFT IFSC). The participants reaffirmed their strong commitment to the Indian market and expressed their intention to sustain and expand their investments in India, reflecting continued confidence in the country’s long-term growth prospects.
The visit also advanced dialogue on financial connectivity and emerging financial technologies. In meetings with Singapore’s financial authorities, including the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), both sides exchanged views on frontier technologies such as tokenisation of financial assets, digital money, central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), interoperability and trusted settlement arrangements. Singapore expressed its keenness to share its experience in asset tokenisation. The discussions provided an opportunity to explore further cooperation between the financial authorities of the two countries on emerging technologies and their application in financial markets.
Engagements with businesses also covered opportunities arising from India’s expanding semiconductor and AI ecosystems. Discussions included investment under the India Semiconductor Mission, development of skilled manpower, industry-linked training and AI skilling initiatives, and the application of AI in banking and financial services. Other areas included renewable energy, electric mobility, aviation maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO), food security and processing, sustainable finance, and healthcare infrastructure.
Engagement with the Singapore Business Federation (SBF) focused on strengthening business-to-business linkages through targeted business matching and visits by Singapore business delegations to India for meaningful interactions with Indian businesses and State Governments. SBF highlighted potential areas for collaboration, including semiconductor supply chains, MRO, food security and food processing.
The visit reaffirmed the depth of the India–Singapore partnership and the shared interest in translating ongoing policy dialogue into greater investment, business engagement and financial cooperation. The wide-ranging interactions with Singapore’s political leadership, institutional investors, financial institutions and businesses helped showcase India’s growth and investment opportunities, identify areas of mutual interest and strengthen channels for follow-up engagement. The discussions are expected to support continued efforts to mobilise long-term capital, deepen financial connectivity and advance cooperation in emerging and strategic sectors.
Smt. Sitharaman was accompanied by the CEO of the National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF), the Chairperson of the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA), and senior officials of the Department of Economic Affairs.
